news.title: The 2028 Race Is About to Start and JD Vance Has Already Won (Probably)
news.text:
We’ve still got the midterms to get through, so maybe it’s too early to talk about the 2028 presidential primary, but then again, why not? After all, the second that 2026 is decided, the 2028 cycle begins. It’s inevitable. Heck, it’s already happening. You can see politicians jostling for position, lofting trial balloons, and generally demonstrating how they are utterly overcome by delusion.

Here’s the fact: the nominee is going to be JD Vance unless either JD Vance or Donald Trump decides it’s not going to be JD Vance.

No debate. There’s no actual contest. That’s how it’s going to work out. That’s the only way it can work out. Anybody telling you anything else is wrong. They may be wrong because they’re crazy. They may be wrong because they’re dumb. They may be wrong because they’re delusional. Maybe they’re wrong and know they’re wrong but are saying it anyway because they think it’s to their advantage. But the truth is indisputable. Donald Trump is going to pick the next Republican nominee, and right now it’s JD Vance.

Now, of course, JD Vance might decide not to do it. He’s got a young and growing family, and his wife might not want to put up with this insanity. She might not want to live with a husband who is in the sights of every leftist sociopath out there with a gun and a grudge. They want to murder us, which we can tell by the fact that they have murdered us in the past and would’ve had a higher body count if they could shoot straight.

Alternatively, JD Vance might not think that 2028 is a great opportunity for Republicans. He’s young, and he’ll have many chances down the road, potentially. There’s always the chance that 2028 is his peak, and that somebody else will come along to grab the spotlight, but he might want to take a bye if things aren’t looking great and the administration is unpopular. But the thing is that things probably will look great.

Oh, if the Democrats take one or both houses of Congress, that’s going to be a mess, but that’s not going to reflect on Trump. That’s going to reflect on the Democrats. You’ll have a ravenous, roiling cauldron of left-wing insanity, weirdness, and perversion going on every single day, which will serve to remind people of what the alternative to sober, successful Republican rule is. In 2026, they’re doing everything they can not to remind people what they will do once they get power again. They won’t be able to hide it once they have a little; they’ve already promised to do nothing but investigate political enemies and try to impeach Trump. After the third, fourth, or even fifth impeachment, people are going to get a little tired of that nonsense. Political onanism only goes so far.

But the bigger problem for the Democrats is that Trump’s economy is going to start kicking in over the next year. The new golden age got delayed by trouble with the Fed and with the Iran war, but the economy is fundamentally sound and improving. Things are going to start rocking. We’ve seen this before, those of us who aren’t 12. Remember 1982? The great Ronald Reagan got crushed in the 1982 midterms because his economic policies hadn’t kicked in yet. But by 1984, they had, and it was morning in America, buddy. Reagan won every state except Minnesota, and the way Minnesota is going, that might be up for grabs in 2028, too.

Also, the Iran war is going to be finished by 2028, while Cuba’s going to be free; communists will be swinging from the lampposts — that’s Marco Rubio’s consolation prize for skipping the 2028 cycle. The problem for the Democrats is all they can do is stop legislation and complain. Trump’s going to get the credit for the economy, and the Democrats will have a track record of opposing everything that led to the golden age. And that means the next Republicans are going to have a solid opportunity in 2028, particularly if the Democrats nominate Kamala Harris, and what are the chances of them picking a creepy white sociopath like Gavin Newsom over a black communist woman?

I don’t think JD will let this opportunity go, and unless he gets in a big fight with Donald Trump — always a possibility — Donald Trump will anoint him, and most everyone in the GOP will fall in line.

But what about the guys who won’t? What about the guys who, despite JD's inevitability, throw their hat in the ring?

There would be two main kinds of competing primary opponents, the bitter and the delusional. Start with the bitter. These are the guys who’ve been rejected. These are the guys who’ve presented themselves to Republican voters and been soundly rejected. They’re terrible. They just don’t fit where we are, and it makes them mad that the peasants are revolting. How dare the proles not recognize their manifest superiority and entitlement to greater glory!

There are a bunch of these malcontents out there. I’m sure we’ll see Mike Pence give it another whirl; he’s the party guest who doesn’t know when to leave, except he doesn’t drink, so he didn’t even provide the entertainment that a drunk would. How about Don Bacon, that guy from Nebraska? He was an Air Force general, which says everything you need to know; rarely do you meet anyone else who is simultaneously so pleased with himself and so bereft of any reason to be a general officer jumping into politics. He’s pretty sure that the GOP needs amnesty and submission, but no one’s biting at that bait. That’s why he didn’t bother running again in his blue-leaning district; it wasn’t the Democrat votes he was worried about earning.

And then there are guys like Thomas Massie, the herpes of American politics — he’s gross and never goes away. He does speak for a constituency, though, the geniuses who are convinced there’s a giant Epstein conspiracy out there somewhere that Tommyboy will someday disclose — someday—and who also blame Jews for their inability to satisfy a woman. They are the perfect demographic for a cynical demagogue who does the impossible and makes libertarians look even more ridiculous.

Then there’s the delusional crew. These are good guys. They’ve come through for us in the past. They’d make good presidents. They’re just not going to make good presidents starting in January 2029, unless JD bows out for some reason, and Marco Rubio then bows out for some reason. That’s a lot of bowing, and it’s just not going to happen. I mean, it could happen. And they might come riding to the inauguration in a glittering silver carriage pulled by unicorns.

JD Vance is already taking some swipes at Ted Cruz and vice versa. I think Ted Cruz is a huge asset to the Republican Party. I did something for Ted Cruz that a guy like me — significantly Scottish — rarely does and gave him money the last time he ran for president, so I am speaking as a supporter. What I have to say as a supporter is this: Ted, buddy, you have zero chance of winning the nomination, so don’t waste our time and your dignity trying to win it in 2028. I know that Ted Cruz really, really wants to be president, and I think he’d make a good president, but over the next couple of cycles, a Ted Cruz presidency is the American political equivalent of “fetch.” It just ain’t going to happen.

John Kennedy is the senator from Louisiana who specializes in cornpone country-fried aphorisms and the surgical cross-examination of witnesses at committee hearings. Far from being some backward rube, this guy was a sensational trial lawyer (I read and appreciated his Louisiana Law Review pieces on products liability) and has made noises like he might give it a shot. OK, I like the guy. He’s doing a good job when he’s not going on weird, Trump-targeted tangents like pushing to outlaw naming buildings after living people five weeks before the midterms, but he doesn’t need to be president in 2028. Maybe somebody told him he’d have a shot, but he’s smart enough not to listen.

And there’s Brian Kemp from Georgia, who seems to think he’s got a shot. I don’t want to hear one damn thing about his presidential aspirations unless he delivers the governorship for Rick Jackson and the Senate seat for Mike Collins. And after that, I still don’t want to hear one damn thing about his presidential aspirations. He’s just not going to be president in 2028, and probably not ever.

Other good guys who get mentioned are Doug Burgum, Tom Cotton, Ron DeSantis, and several others. Again, all good guys. They all would make a terrific chief executive. But none of them is going to make a terrific chief executive next cycle. They should focus on doing the jobs that they’re doing. They can try again down the road.

With the emphasis on “down the road.” See, there’s a big roadblock in front of 2028. It’s Donald Trump, and he’s directing traffic on that figurative road. Right now, the only guy who’s driving through the barrier is JD Vance. You might not like it. You might not dig it. But that’s the way it is. And the sooner we all get that through our heads, the sooner we can start focusing on winning in 2028 — after we win in 2026, of course.

news.title: Obama hosts fundraiser with Senate Democrats weeks before midterms
news.text: Washington – Former President Barack Obama headlined a fundraiser for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Wednesday night to discuss the stakes of the upcoming midterm election.The event featured a conversation between Obama and Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, vice chair of the DSCC, about Democrats' efforts to flip the Senate. "I think he is just such a voice for our country, and of both realism and practical optimism, and I think we need that right now," Blunt Rochester told CBS News. "And I think he also lays the foundation for the significance of this election."Senate Democrats have become increasingly optimistic about their prospects this fall after several races shifted toward the party in recent weeks, including in deep-red states like Texas and Ohio that are considered toss-ups, according to CBS News' battleground tracker. "We do not want to be overconfident, but what we're seeing in state after state after state is that people are sick of Trump, they're sick of the Republican Senate going along with them, and they see the clear divisions we have drawn between what we stand for and what they stand for," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told CBS News last month. "That has put us on the edge of victory." Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate. Democrats would need to pick up four seats to gain control of the upper chamber. Meanwhile, Republicans have argued they still have a path to hold on to the Senate."Right now, there's a lot of noise, there always is in the political atmosphere — some of it's created by our opponents," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a South Dakota Republican, told reporters before the body went on recess. "But if we can stay focused, talk about the future and the two paths over the course of the next several weeks, based on our record of accomplishment, things we got done, things we still need to do, we've got a great argument."One key target for both parties is Michigan. Democrats are trying to hold the seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Gary Peters while Republicans see it as a prime pickup opportunity. An exclusive CBS Detroit poll, conducted by Mitchell Research and Communications, shows Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed with a narrow advantage over GOP challenger and former Rep. Mike Rogers. Obama is expected to campaign with El-Sayed and other Democratic candidates in the Wolverine State later this month. A source familiar with the former president's thinking said his strategy this fall is "driven by where he can move the needle with Democrats and persuadable voters." The former president has also taped two dozen ads for Senate and gubernatorial candidates around the country. Last month, he participated in the second of two fundraisers with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, where he pressed Democrats to do more on the issue of artificial intelligence."Certainly if I were running for president next year, this would be one of my central agendas, and I would have a very clear plan, and I would talk about this, and I would say, 'Here's our plan for safety, here's our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this,'" Obama said. "I would be thinking about the economic impacts in very concrete ways and understanding: What does it mean if there's going to be job displacement? Where is that going to hit? How are we going to respond?" Jeffries told CBS News he has remained in contact with Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris and expects both to be engaged through Election Day. The minority leader, who is poised to become the first Black House speaker if Democrats win control of the lower chamber, predicted that House Democrats would "take back the majority" this fall. "It's an all-hands-on-deck effort," Jeffries said.
news.summary: Former President Barack Obama headlined a fundraiser for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Wednesday night to discuss the stakes of the upcoming midterm election.

news.title: Tinubu’s extended absence
news.text:
NIGERIA has a disturbing habit of allowing those in power to treat constitutional restraints as inconveniences rather than obligations. Once again, the country is confronted with questions over presidential absence, constitutional compliance and the willingness of its institutions to hold the powerful to account.

At some point in September, President Bola Tinubu, Vice-President Kashim Shettima and Senate President Godswill Akpabio were all out of the country. That unusual coincidence alone should have triggered serious questions about constitutional responsibility and the functioning of government.

Instead, Nigerians were left with familiar explanations and little sense of urgency.

Tinubu embarked on a three-week European trip on August 30 and was expected to return on September 21. He did not. He extended his stay in France by another week, turning what was announced as a working vacation into a prolonged absence.

That immediately raises an important constitutional question: when a President is away for an extended period, what formal arrangements are made for the exercise of presidential authority?

The Presidency has previously argued that the President can perform his duties from anywhere in the world. That argument, however, does not answer the specific requirements of Section 145 of the 1999 Constitution.

Section 145(1) provides that whenever the President proceeds on vacation or is otherwise unable to discharge the functions of his office, he shall transmit a written declaration to the President of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives. Until he transmits a declaration to the contrary, the Vice-President is to perform the functions of President as Acting President.

That provision is not ornamental. It exists to guarantee continuity, certainty and constitutional order whenever the President is away or unable to perform his functions.

Nigeria has painfully experienced the consequences of ignoring that principle.

During the prolonged medical absence of the late President Umaru Yar’Adua in 2009 and 2010, power was not formally transferred to his deputy, Goodluck Jonathan. Then Attorney-General and Minister of Justice, Michael Aondoakaa, similarly argued that the President could perform his duties from anywhere in the world. That is blatantly absurd.

The result was a constitutional crisis that eventually forced the National Assembly to invoke the Doctrine of Necessity in February 2010, allowing Jonathan to assume the functions of Acting President.

The Buhari administration followed a similar pattern. In 2019, when President Muhammadu Buhari travelled to London on a “private visit” without formally transferring power to Vice-President Yemi Osinbajo, his spokesman, Garba Shehu, maintained that Buhari could exercise his authority from wherever he was.

Seven years later, Nigeria should not still be having this argument.

The Constitution provides a mechanism for dealing with presidential absence. Section 145(2) further provides for action by the National Assembly where a President fails to transmit the required declaration and remains away beyond the stipulated period.

The National Assembly therefore has a constitutional responsibility in such circumstances. It cannot simply look away because the occupant of the Presidency is politically powerful.

Unfortunately, Nigeria’s political class has repeatedly demonstrated an unhealthy reluctance to enforce constitutional restraints against those in power.

That is wrong.

A Constitution that is enforced only when convenient is not really a Constitution; it becomes a suggestion.

There is also the question of Section 143, which provides the constitutional procedure for the removal of a President or Vice-President for gross misconduct.

It should not be casually claimed that a presidential absence automatically amounts to an impeachable offence. But neither should the National Assembly behave as though constitutional breaches, where established, are beyond scrutiny.

The issue is accountability.

Presidents are not monarchs. They do not possess unlimited discretion. They hold office under a Constitution, and the powers they exercise belong to the Nigerian state, not to them personally.

That principle becomes even more important when presidential travel involves enormous public expenditure.

Why should a Nigerian President routinely spend extended periods on “working vacations” or “private visits” abroad when Nigeria has official facilities for presidential retreats and government work? 

What exactly is a “private visit” when the traveller is the President of Nigeria, accompanied by security personnel, officials and other members of the presidential entourage, with public resources inevitably involved?

Nigerians deserve answers.

Parking the presidential aircraft at a European airport for weeks does not come free. Neither do the security arrangements, logistics and other costs associated with maintaining the President and his entourage abroad.

This is happening in a country struggling to fund essential public services and where the government repeatedly pleads fiscal constraints.

There is nothing wrong with a President travelling. International diplomacy requires it. So do bilateral meetings, multilateral engagements and other legitimate state functions.

But a vacation is a different matter.

There is a reason responsible governments make clear arrangements for the temporary transfer of authority when their leaders are unavailable. Constitutional certainty is more important than personal convenience.

The United States provides a useful illustration. On November 19, 2021, President Joe Biden invoked Section 3 of the 25th Amendment to temporarily transfer presidential powers to Vice-President Kamala Harris while he underwent anaesthesia for a routine colonoscopy. Harris exercised the presidential powers for about 85 minutes before they were returned to Biden.

This demonstrates that constitutional clarity does not become less important because the period involved is short.

Nigeria should understand that lesson.

There have also been persistent public speculations about whether some of Tinubu’s foreign trips have had medical considerations. Such speculation should not be presented as fact without evidence. But neither can the Presidency reasonably expect Nigerians to ignore questions surrounding prolonged presidential absences.

The health and availability of a sitting President inevitably have a public dimension because the office carries enormous constitutional, security and economic responsibilities.

The Presidency therefore owes Nigerians clear and factual communication. Its media managers should stop treating legitimate questions as hostile attacks and start treating transparency as part of their responsibility to the public.

The taxpayers who finance the Presidency have a right to know why their President is away for extended periods, what official business is being conducted and what constitutional arrangements are in place.

More importantly, the National Assembly must remember that it is a constitutional institution, not an appendage of the executive.

Its members swear allegiance to the Constitution, not to the President.

If the National Assembly cannot insist on compliance when constitutional provisions are being tested by the executive, who will?

Nigeria has spent decades paying lip service to the rule of law while allowing political power to determine the practical limits of accountability.

That culture must change.

The President must respect the Constitution. The Vice-President must respect it. The National Assembly must enforce it. And the citizens must insist that they do.

Nigeria does not need more presidential explanations after the fact. It needs institutions strong enough to prevent constitutional ambiguity in the first place.

A President’s vacation cannot become a constitutional vacation.

No officeholder, however powerful, should be allowed to behave as though the Constitution is suspended whenever it becomes inconvenient.

Until Nigeria learns that lesson, democracy will remain less about the rule of law than about the discretion of those who happen to hold power.

news.title: Obama is set to get more involved in the midterms, starting with an appearance alongside Abdul El-Sayed
news.text: Former President Barack Obama will campaign alongside Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit later this month, lending his support to the progressive nominee after a bruising Democratic primary exposed divisions within the party.Obama will appear with El-Sayed at an Oct. 24 rally that will also feature other top Democratic candidates in Michigan, including Jocelyn Benson, the party's nominee for governor. Obama is getting significantly more involved in the midterm elections, with additional campaign stops and advertisements expected to come in the closing weeks, according to plans shared first with The Associated Press.The Detroit event is a notable show of support for El-Sayed, who defeated moderate Rep. Haley Stevens in an August primary and has since worked to consolidate Democratic support in his race against Republican Mike Rogers. The open seat is expected to be among a handful that will decide which party controls the majority next year.Obama taped two dozen ads last week for Democratic candidates for governor and Senate that will be released in the coming days and weeks, in addition to more campaign stops soon to be announced.He appeared earlier this year in a campaign ad with Iowa Senate candidate Josh Turek and campaigned in Texas with Senate candidate James Talarico and the candidate for governor, Gina Hinojosa. This week, he will headline a Washington fundraiser supporting Democratic Senate candidates.RELATED STORY | Trump takes midterm push to Nebraska amid economic concerns among farmersObama aims to help El-Sayed shore up support in a key areaEl-Sayed defeated Stevens by less than a percentage point in a primary that became a national test of the Democratic Party’s ideological direction. El-Sayed drew support from leading progressives, including Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders and Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York. Stevens was backed by Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer.Some ads that supported Stevens showed Obama praising her, and she outperformed El-Sayed in Wayne County, winning about 51% of the Democratic primary vote compared with 45% for El-Sayed. The county includes Detroit, where more than three-quarters of residents are Black.Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian person to serve as vice president, campaigned with El-Sayed last month.Now the Oct. 24 rally with Obama, the first Black president, could give El-Sayed a boost on the first day of Michigan’s required early in-person voting period. Obama spoke with El-Sayed by phone following his primary victory.It will also be a boost for the other candidates in what is one of the most consequential elections in recent Michigan history. There are open races for governor, secretary of state and attorney general, in addition to control of the state legislature being at play.Benson, who will also appear with Obama, is facing Republican Rep. John James in the race for governor.Benson and James are set to debate for the first time on Tuesday, and El-Sayed and Rogers are scheduled to debate for the first time on Oct. 8.RELATED NEWS | FCC considers allowing more political robocalls before midtermsObama returns to the campaign trail for the closing stretchObama has been selective in his involvement in the midterms so far, but his planned ramp-up in the final weeks follows a pattern from recent elections. He campaigned in Detroit on Oct. 22 during the 2024 presidential election and was in the city Oct. 29 during the 2022 midterms.His campaign appearances can draw large crowds and prominent guests. Rapper Eminem introduced Obama at his Detroit rally in 2024.This week, he will headline an event with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee that will include a conversation with Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester. That follows a September event with the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

news.title: Can $1 billion power Republicans to victory in the midterms?
news.text:
WASHINGTON — Republicans are entering the final month of the midterm campaign increasingly anxious that the $1 billion at their disposal may not be enough to fend off sweeping losses as the party reckons with President Donald Trump’s unpopularity, persistent cost concerns and the fallout from the war in Iran.

The cash advantage, spread out across a half-dozen groups, is driven largely by the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc., which had nearly $416 million in cash on hand at the end of August and began stepping up its spending on critical races in September.

But that money may have come too late, forcing the president’s group to pay much higher rates because of the shrinking availability of air time. Four Republican Senate campaign officials said groups that reserved advertising time last spring paid much lower rates than MAGA Inc. and its affiliated groups.

Instead, by waiting until September, Trump-connected organizations are sometimes paying more than five times what they would have spent if they acted earlier.

A representative of MAGA Inc. familiar with the group’s strategy said its spending has allowed Republicans to keep races more competitive than they would have been otherwise. In some cases, the group has been the only one on the air criticizing Democratic candidates.

The MAGA Inc. representative and the Republican Senate campaign officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal strategy.

The challenge is acute in places like Texas, where Trump will travel on Wednesday for the second time in a week to stump for Republican Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign. The state hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1988, yet MAGA Inc. has spent more than $22 million in the past month, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact.

Another group, Texas PAC, which is aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, has spent more than $83 million on advertising in the past month, an extraordinary amount to protect what’s normally a safe Republican seat.

One of those advertisements, which featured Paxton’s estranged wife saying she’s supporting the full Republican ticket, aired across the United States last weekend during a football game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Houston Texans.

Candidates are charged a lower advertising rate than outside groups, so the late infusion of super PAC cash has come at a steep price.

MAGA Inc., which is running ads primarily on streaming services, has been charged roughly $894 per airing, according to AdImpact, while Texas PAC has been charged roughly $809 for a mix of broadcast and streaming. That compares with about $290 for Democratic nominee James Talarico’s campaign, also on broadcast and streaming.

Those averages mask some of the more glaring disparities. For example, during a football game last month, Texas PAC was charged $450,000 to air a single spot in the Austin market. Talarico’s campaign paid $50,000 for a spot during the same game in the same market, according to AdImpact.

Elections are a referendum on the power of money

The 2026 campaign is shaping up as a referendum on the power of money in American politics. Democrats freely acknowledge their disadvantage, relying instead on anti-Trump sentiment among voters and targeted messaging on issues like corruption. Some Republicans, meanwhile, are open about the challenge of trying to spend their way out of a tough campaign at this late stage.

Neil Newhouse, a longtime Republican pollster, echoed concerns that his party was deploying its cash too late.

“After the votes are counted, I think we’re going to find the most effective advertising in terms of communicating message and moving voters and poll numbers, the most effective time was advertising that happened well before Labor Day, not after it,” he said. “A million dollars of advertising in October is a drop in the bucket.”

Thune’s group began pulling back in North Carolina last week, a sign of the party’s challenge in the Senate race there. The state’s outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis has been increasingly vocal about his party’s vulnerabilities and recently said that, even with a strong cash advantage, “in the last month, you pretty much have to place your bets.”

“If we have endless resources, then we should spend endlessly in every state,” he said. “Absent endless resources, you’ve got to make data-driven decisions about where you can win.”

The midterms mark the first national election since the Supreme Court in June erased limits on how much political parties can spend in coordination with candidates for Congress and president, injecting even more money into a political system already awash in cash.

Money alone doesn’t translate into victory

There’s plenty of evidence that money alone doesn’t translate into victory.

Democrat Kamala Harris entered the final stretch of the 2024 campaign with significantly more money than Trump but went on to lose every critical swing state and the White House. Elon Musk’s $25 million didn’t lift his preferred candidate to a Wisconsin Supreme Court seat last year. And Tom Steyer didn’t advance to the general election in the California governor’s race despite pumping $216 million of his own money into the campaign.

The $1 billion that Republicans have amassed compares with roughly $579 million held by a comparable collection of major Democratic groups.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said his party is facing an “obscene” amount of spending that could swamp them in the midterms.

“We’re never going to have as much money as them,” he said in an interview. “I sum up the election in this sentence: Can a massive Republican advantage in money beat a massive Democratic advantage in better candidates and political climate? I bet it can’t.”

In addition to Texas, Democrats have mounted competitive Senate campaigns in states like Ohio, Maine, Iowa and Michigan. A similar dynamic has emerged in governors’ races from Florida and Georgia to Wisconsin, Ohio and Nevada.

Former President Barack Obama is stepping up his involvement in the midterms and will headline a fundraiser for Senate candidates on Wednesday.

In the House, Democrats are growing so confident they can retake the majority that they’re expanding their targets deeper into traditionally Republican districts in Arkansas and Tennessee. But a lack of money could limit their gains.

“We absolutely need to spend enough to get our message out,” said Rep. Suzan DelBene of Washington, who chairs the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. “And district by district, we are.”

Trump turns to his bond with supporters

From his earliest days as an unlikely political figure, Trump has consistently overcome expectations. Facing daunting prospects heading into the final weeks of his last midterm, he’s betting he can again outwit political gravity, relying in large part on the deep bond he’s built with supporters.

He has stepped up his campaign rallies in recent weeks, traveling to deep red territory to galvanize the party faithful. At events like the one this past weekend in Vandalia, Ohio, the crowd was enthusiastic and cheered at the lines that have become Trump staples over the years, particularly when he dips into profanity. The high school gymnasium that held the event was packed, though crowds began emptying out about halfway through the 90-minute rally.

In the closing minutes of a speech Monday in Grand Island, Neb., the president revived his plea that supporters who have stood so fervently by him pretend as if he is on the ballot one more time.

“In a true way, I am running,” he said. “We have to keep it going.”

Debra Messing has received quite a bit of backlash for supporting the Trump-backed Republican candidate for New York Governor despite decades of being a devout Democrat.

The 58-year-old Will & Grace star met up with a member of the GOP, Bruce Blakeman, to reveal public support for him just weeks before his showdown with Democratic incumbent Kathy Hochul in the 2026 election.

news.title: David Jolly Within Striking Distance of Byron Donalds: Florida Poll
news.text: Democrat David Jolly is trailing Republican Representative Byron Donalds by just 2 points in the race for Florida governor, according to a new YouGov poll, the latest sign that the contest to succeed Governor Ron DeSantis is tighter than many expected. The survey of 3,813 likely voters, conducted September 28 to October 5, found Donalds at 47 percent and Jolly at 45 percent, with 7 percent undecided. The gap falls within the poll's margin of error of plus or minus 2.7 percentage points. Newsweek reached out to both campaigns via email for comment. Florida has not elected a Democratic governor since Lawton Chiles won reelection in 1994, and Republicans have spent the past decade turning the onetime battleground into one of their most dependable states. President Donald Trump, who moved his legal residence from New York to his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach during his first term, carried Florida by about 13 points in 2024. A close race for Trump's pick in his own home state would say a good deal about how much the national mood has moved before the November 3 midterms. What the YouGov Poll Shows The YouGov sample leans Republican by registration, 45 percent to 31 percent, and respondents said they backed Trump over Kamala Harris by 11 points in 2024. Even so, 54 percent of likely voters said they disapprove of the job Trump is doing as president, including 49 percent who strongly disapprove. Forty-six percent approve. Jolly's support is concentrated among younger voters. He leads Donalds 59 percent to 28 percent among voters ages 18 to 29 and 54 percent to 35 percent among those 30 to 44. Donalds leads 55 percent to 40 percent among voters 65 and older, who make up 39 percent of the poll's likely electorate. The poll also found Jolly ahead among Hispanic voters, 49 percent to 44 percent, a group that swung sharply toward Republicans in DeSantis' 2022 reelection and Trump's 2024 win. Donalds leads white voters without a college degree 59 percent to 33 percent, while white college graduates are nearly split, 47 percent for Donalds and 45 percent for Jolly. There is little crossover voting, and what exists favors the Democrat: 5 percent of Trump's 2024 voters back Jolly, against 1 percent of Harris voters who back Donalds. A Mixed Picture in Earlier Polling The broader picture is less settled. Some recent surveys show Jolly narrowly ahead, while others give Donalds a high single-digit or double-digit lead. Forecasters have steadily moved the race toward Democrats, but prediction markets still treat Donalds as a clear favorite. The other newest survey in the race came from Mason-Dixon Polling & Strategy. Its poll for NBC 6 Miami and Telemundo, taken September 28 to October 1 among 625 likely voters, had Donalds up 7 points, 48 percent to 41 percent. Two Change Research polls have pointed the other way. A survey for Freedom Project USA, conducted September 25 to 27, showed Jolly leading 48 percent to 46 percent, and an earlier September poll from the firm had him up 47 percent to 44 percent. A Hart Research survey for the Democratic Governors Association, released in late August, put Jolly at 46 percent and Donalds at 45 percent. Stetson University's Center for Public Opinion Research has the widest recent gap: Donalds 51 percent, Jolly 39 percent, in a survey taken September 14 to 21. The University of North Florida's July poll was tighter, with Donalds ahead 46 percent to 41 percent. Florida's recent history offers a caution for Democrats reading those numbers. In 2018, final polling averages showed Democrat Andrew Gillum ahead of DeSantis by several points, but DeSantis won by less than half a percentage point. In 2022, polls showed DeSantis leading Charlie Crist, another former Republican running as a Democrat, by low double digits, and he won by more than 19 points. Election forecasters have nonetheless shifted their ratings. The Cook Political Report moved the race from "Solid Republican" to "Likely Republican" in late August. Sabato's Crystal Ball, which rated the race "Safe Republican" until July, now has it at "Lean Republican." Decision Desk HQ went furthest, moving Florida from "Lean Republican" to "Toss-up." "Cook is saying the contest is no longer a complete lock," Craig Agranoff, a political professor at Florida Atlantic University, told Newsweek after the shift, "mainly because David Jolly is a former Republican with a ticket that can talk to independents." How Florida Became a Republican Stronghold Florida decided the 2000 presidential election by 537 votes and remained a perennial swing state through 2016. That changed quickly. Republicans overtook Democrats in voter registration in 2021, and the gap has since widened. As of June 30, the state had about 5.57 million registered Republicans, 4.04 million Democrats and 3.32 million voters with no party affiliation, according to the Florida Division of Elections. DeSantis' 2022 landslide, which included carrying heavily Hispanic Miami-Dade County, turned him into a national figure and briefly a rival to Trump for the party's 2024 nomination. Trump then won the state by double digits. Florida Republicans now hold every statewide office, and the state has become a pipeline for the administration: former Senator Marco Rubio left his seat to become secretary of state, and DeSantis appointed then-Attorney General Ashley Moody to replace him. The tension between Trump and DeSantis also shaped this year's primary. Trump endorsed Donalds early, while DeSantis stood behind Lieutenant Governor Jay Collins. Donalds won the August 18 primary with 47.8 percent of the vote. Donalds' campaign says it has raised more than $90 million, a financial edge that Jolly has not come close to matching. Ryan Smith, the campaign's chief strategist, dismissed the Sabato move in July. "Florida is a red state and will remain a red state in November when Byron Donalds is elected the next Governor," he said. Democrats See an Opening Democrats point to recent special elections as evidence that the state's rightward drift has stalled. In March, first-time candidate Emily Gregory flipped Florida House District 87, which includes Mar-a-Lago, defeating Trump-endorsed Republican Jon Maples. A Republican had carried the district by 19 points in 2024. Donalds had filmed an endorsement for Maples. Jolly, a former Republican congressman from Pinellas County who left the party during Trump's first term, has built his campaign around affordability, housing costs and opposition to new data centers. His running mate is former Democratic Representative Gwen Graham. "For the first time, the Florida governor's race is officially a toss up," Jolly wrote on social media after the Decision Desk HQ move. "Florida is winnable." "In this change election, Florida is ready to elect a Democrat," Mark Riddle, a senior adviser to Jolly, said in a statement. Donalds' camp has shrugged off the ratings changes. After the Cook move, communications director Gates McGavick posted "Nice try, guys" on X and said the campaign looked forward "to checking in with @CookPolitical on November 4th." Angie Nixon Faces a Steeper Climb in the Senate Race Florida's Senate race, a special election for the remainder of Rubio's term, looks somewhat less competitive. The YouGov poll found Moody leading Democrat Angie Nixon 49 percent to 44 percent, with 5 percent undecided after allocation. Both candidates' supporters appear locked in: 95 percent of Nixon voters and 94 percent of Moody voters said their minds are made up. Nixon, a state representative from Jacksonville and self-described democratic socialist, won the August primary with about 55 percent of the vote, defeating retired Army Lieutenant Colonel Alexander Vindman despite being outspent by roughly $17 million. Since the primary, the numbers have been all over the place. St. Pete Polls, surveying for Florida Politics, had Moody at 45.2 percent and Nixon at 44.8 percent. Change Research's poll for Freedom Project USA put Moody ahead by a single point, 48 to 47. Quantus Insights gave her a 7-point lead, and the July UNF survey had her up 8. Nixon has attacked Moody over a grand jury report that named the senator in a plan to steer $10 million from a Medicaid settlement to the Hope Florida Foundation, a nonprofit created by Florida first lady Casey DeSantis. Nixon called for Moody's resignation after the report's release. Moody remains a heavy favorite in prediction markets, which gave her a better than 90 percent chance of winning in late August. No Democrat has won a Senate race in Florida since Bill Nelson in 2012. Early voting begins later this month, and the election is November 3.
news.summary: Democrat David Jolly trails GOP nominee Byron Donalds by 2 points in Florida's governor race, a new poll finds.

news.title: Gina Hinojosa Chance of Beating Greg Abbott Flips With Pollsters
news.text: As much of the attention in Texas this fall has focused on the U.S. Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton, another statewide contest has been tightening under the radar: Governor Greg Abbott's bid for a record fourth term. A new YouGov poll of 3,622 likely voters, conducted September 28 through October 5, has Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa narrowly ahead of Abbott, 48 percent to 47 percent, with 5 percent undecided. The margin of error is plus or minus 3 percentage points. Pollsters have traded leads all fall. A year ago, few Texas Republicans would have predicted that Abbott, who has won each of his three races for governor by double digits, would be scrapping for votes less than four weeks before Election Day. If Hinojosa wins, she would be the first Democrat to hold the office since Ann Richards left in 1995. If Abbott wins, he would be on track to become the longest-serving governor in Texas history. Newsweek reached out to Hinojosa and Abbott campaigns for comment Wednesday. Hinojosa Gets Strong Support From Black and Latino Voters Age is the sharpest dividing line in the YouGov survey. Hinojosa takes 64 percent of voters under 30 and 58 percent of those aged 30 to 44. Among Texans 65 and older, Abbott wins 61 percent to 36 percent. Gender splits the electorate almost evenly in both directions, with women backing Hinojosa 52 percent to 42 percent and men favoring Abbott by an identical margin. On race and ethnicity, Hinojosa leads Hispanic voters 58 percent to 37 percent and Black voters 80 percent to 12 percent. Abbott carries white voters by 21 points, a lead built mostly on white Texans without a college degree, who back him 68 percent to 29 percent. White college graduates are essentially a coin flip at 47 percent for Hinojosa and 46 percent for Abbott. Republican strategist Mike Madrid, who has spent years tracking Hispanic voting behavior, said the numbers reflect something the political establishment has been slow to grasp. "People, I think, broadly are failing to understand that the Latino vote is the largest swing vote in America," Madrid told Newsweek in an interview. Democrats are running a little better in the Senate race. Talarico leads Paxton 50 percent to 44 percent in the same poll, and he wins 97 percent of Harris voters to Hinojosa's 95 percent. Abbott, meanwhile, holds 84 percent of 2024 Trump voters, two points more than Paxton. One caveat on the comparison: YouGov allocated undecided voters in the Senate question but did not do so for governor, which helps explain why 5 percent remain undecided there compared with 3 percent in the Senate race. Then there is Trump. Only 44 percent of Texas likely voters approve of the job he is doing, and 51 percent strongly disapprove, in a sample that says it backed him over Kamala Harris by 12 points in 2024. What Earlier Polls Show Which candidate is ahead depends a lot on which pollster you read. In June, a New York Times/Siena College poll of 656 likely voters found Abbott with the backing of 51 percent of voters and Hinojosa with 44 percent. When Times/Siena went back into the field from September 21 to 30, Hinojosa led 49 percent to 46 percent among 615 likely voters. Marist University's September 17 to 20 survey of 1,139 registered voters landed on the same 49-46 result. ReconMR and the Siena Research Institute also showed Hinojosa leading 49 percent to 45 percent, a reversal from July, when the same poll had Abbott ahead by a single point. The Fox News poll, conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research from September 24 to 28, put Abbott up 52 percent to 47 percent among 881 likely voters. Big Data Poll and Slingshot Strategies each had the governor ahead by 4 or 5 points, as did a Stratus Intelligence poll paid for by the Republican group Texans for a Conservative Majority. In between sit an N+ Univision/YouGov poll that found the two candidates deadlocked at 47 percent and an Overton Insights/Texas Public Policy Foundation survey with Abbott ahead 46.9 percent to 45.8 percent. Over the summer, the governor's cushion was wider. Abbott led by 7 points in a University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll in early June, and a late July Texas Southern University poll found him leading 49 percent to 43 percent. No public poll since mid-September has shown him up by more than 5. A Blue Texas? It Might Happen Democrats have been promising a breakthrough in Texas for three decades. No Democrat has won statewide office there since 1994, and Trump carried the state by 13 points in 2024. Abbott beat Beto O'Rourke by roughly 11 points in 2022. Hinojosa is a different kind of candidate from O'Rourke. A civil rights and union lawyer who grew up in the Rio Grande Valley, she made her name in the Texas House as the chief antagonist of Abbott's school voucher push, and her campaign has since widened its focus to grocery bills, data centers and what she calls corruption in the governor's office. "Every poll tells the same story: Texans are tired of working more and getting less," Hinojosa said over the summer. Her numbers among Hispanic voters, who swung toward Republicans in 2024, may matter most. Madrid said Washington misread what happened in 2024. "Most people were thinking it was part of this permanent realignment. A lot of people who understand the Latino vote were saying it's not that at all," he said. Independents are also drifting her way, according to ReconMR, which found her with large leads in Austin, Dallas-Fort Worth and San Antonio and Abbott ahead in rural areas. Abbott keeps the upper hand on the issues Republicans have run on for a decade. On securing the border, voters picked him over Hinojosa 53 percent to 39 percent, and he led on keeping Texans safe, while she led on making prices more affordable. He also has far more money. At the end of June, Abbott had about $67 million on hand to Hinojosa's $3 million, though she has said her campaign raised $20 million since January. The Latest on the Race There may never be a debate. Hinojosa accepted an invitation for a one-hour debate on Thursday, October 15, in Fort Worth, hosted by NBCUniversal Television Stations Texas and Hearst Newspapers Texas and broadcast in English and Spanish. Her campaign says Abbott let the deadline pass, and that he also ignored a September debate hosted by Nexstar. Abbott's team has preferred social media. The governor recently posted an image of Hinojosa as a Lotería card, the Mexican bingo game. Campaign spokesperson Eduardo Leal defended the post, calling Hinojosa an "out-of-touch Democrat socialist." From the Hinojosa side, the reply was an invitation. Abbott "has to lie because he's been governor for 12 years," spokesperson Tommy Kubischek said, adding that the governor should make his case at a debate. Hinojosa is also courting voters well outside her party. At the Texas Tribune Festival, she unveiled an ad featuring Lynn Davenport, a self-described MAGA conservative who believed the 2020 election was stolen and now says she will vote for the Democrat. Abbott was invited to the festival and didn't respond. What Happens Next Early voting begins October 19 and ends October 30. Election Day is November 3, and the Fort Worth debate, whether Abbott shows up or not, comes four days before the first ballots are cast. Turnout could decide it. The groups carrying Hinojosa in the YouGov poll, younger voters and Hispanic voters, tend to skip midterms at higher rates than the older white Texans who make up Abbott's base. And the governor has the money to stay on television through the final stretch. Hinojosa's fate may be tied to Talarico's. A Senate race that drives Democratic-leaning voters to the polls would help her more than anything her own campaign can buy.
news.summary: A new YouGov poll has Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa narrowly ahead of Greg Abbott.

news.title: 'Top Gun: Maverick' Star Glen Powell Explains Why He Doesn't Preach Politics: It Divides People
news.text:
The Twisters star Glen Powell says he is not interested in speaking out about politics because the discussion alienates too many people.

In an interview with Esquire magazine, Powell says that his parents were utterly disinterested in politics. And these days, the Chad Powers star says that politics interests him even less, the magazine says.

To Powell, politics are just too divisive.

“Over time, I realized that politics divide people,” he told the magazine.

“People trying to prove their point — for me, it’s the worst version of a conversation,” he continued. “I genuinely do not like the discourse.”

“It’s not as healthy as it once was,” he said, adding that talking politics “is not presently possible. I applaud people for jumping into those things and fighting for what they believe in. If I were a political person, I would be talking about it. For me, my calling is elsewhere.”

Powell has had a series of high-profile roles over the last decade, in films including Top Gun: Maverick, Twisters, and The Running Man. And he has scored a big streaming hit with his football comedy series, Chad Powers, a series he also created along with Michael Waldron.

Powell joins what might be a growing list of actors and entertainers who have finally learned the lesson that speaking out about politics naturally ticks off half their potential fan base.

Action star Dwayne Johnson, for one, learned that lesson after suffering a huge backlash for endorsing Joe Biden, even as he had previously claimed to lean to the center in political ideology. After that debacle, by July of this year, Johnson was pledging to steer clear of politics on the future.

“I’ve learned I’m going to keep my politics to myself. There are moments when, hey, there’s nothing we can’t talk about. If I’m wrong, I’ll tell you I’m wrong. Or if I feel like I got a leg up and this is the right way to go, I’ll share it with you. Politics is omnipresent and it’s forever. I don’t like it. I hate it at times. I hate the slinging. I hate all the bullshit that comes with it,” he said.

After being blasted for supporting Biden, “The Rock” quickly pivoted and refused to make any endorsements when the Democrat Party abandoned Biden and switched allegiance to Kamala Harris.

“My goal is to bring this country together. I believe in that. There will be no endorsement. At this level of influence, I will keep my politics to myself. It is between me and the ballot box,” he said when the party coronated Harris for the 2024 presidential election.

Another top celebrity who recently began backing away from politics is Jennifer Lawrence.

Despite previous vitriolic attacks on Republicans and Donald Trump, the Hunger Games star did an about face late last year by stating that expounding on politics was just making things worse.

Last November, Lawrence said that she has come to the opinion that spouting off about politics does not make a difference. “So, then what am I doing? I’m just sharing my opinion on something that’s going to add fuel to a fire that’s ripping the country apart. We are so divided,” she said.

Others who are begging off on politics include Josh Duhamel, who said actors should avoid upsetting half their audience by talking about politics, and Kevin James, who said he leaves politics to people who are more informed on the issues than he.

news.title: Swing Voters Have Buyer’s Remorse Over Trump — And 1 Candidate Could Get Hit Hard
news.text:
Some Michigan residents who voted for President Donald Trump in the last presidential election expressed buyer’s remorse on Tuesday during an MS NOW focus group.

Multiple swing voters who spoke to the network said they are not willing to vote for Trump-backed Senate candidate Mike Rogers next month over Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed.

“I was surprised that there wasn’t more support or more leaning Rogers in that group,” MS NOW analyst Elise Jordan said after the interviews aired. “You know, these cross-pressure voters, but then you look at some of the polling, and Abdul El-Sayed is pulling more from Trump voters at around 8% than, likewise, than Rogers pulling about 5% of Kamala Harris voters.”

During one panel, she asked the group, “What were you hoping [Trump] would change?”

“I thought, like, run it like a business, more like not just like your family, like bring more in for us for the Americans, get our economy up, and like run it like he wants America to be a wealthy business,” one voter said. “But I just think now it’s a Trump, it’s a Trump business.”

Another Trump voter said she had strong hopes he would make changes in foreign affairs, but she is now “very disappointed.”

“He’s a good liar,” another voter in the room chimed in. 

Rogers, along with other Republican candidates in the midterms, is facing challenges because of his alignment with Trump, whose favorability is sinking as Americans grow sour over the war in Iran and the administration’s handling of the economy. 

A recent Fox News poll shows El-Sayed leading the race with 50%, a slim point above Rogers’ 49%, among likely voters. 

When asked if they would vote for Rogers in the upcoming election, few raised their hands. 

One person who raised her hand for El-Sayed declared, “If I don’t vote for him, I’m not voting.”

“That’s how I would be too. I wouldn’t vote for Mike Rogers,” another voter said.

A voter who raised her hand for Rogers clarified that she’s “not happy about it, but there again, it’s either vote or don’t vote.”

news.title: 'The panic is palpable': El-Sayed facing opposition from key Michigan Democrat groups weeks before election
news.text:
While polling suggests Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is leading the Senate race in Michigan, members of key Democrat-leaning demographics say he hasn't earned their votes, even as absentee ballots have already begun to trickle in.

Like others in the Rust Belt, Michigan is a purple state. Michigan voted for President Donald Trump in 2016 and 2024, but went for President Joe Biden in 2020. It also currently has a Democrat executive branch and state Senate but a Republican House.

'The exodus of Jewish and black Democrats from Conman Abdul El-Sayed's camp exposes his crumbling coalition.'

While Trump won Michigan in 2024, Vice President Kamala Harris carried Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and Oakland County, which has a high Jewish population. That same year, Democrat Elissa Slotkin barely squeaked by Republican Mike Rogers in the U.S. Senate race by just 0.34%.

So it's no wonder that in 2026, El-Sayed and Rogers are in a tough battle for the open seat soon to be vacated by Democrat Sen. Gary Peters.

As of Wednesday afternoon, Blaze News Poll Watch has El-Sayed with an edge of 2.6%, and, according to CNN, El-Sayed has already predicted he will win by seven points.

Yet frank admissions by high-profile Michigan Democrats as well as black and Jewish voters suggest he may actually have some ground to make up in his own party.

Democrat Rep. Hillary Scholten, who represents a district in Western Michigan, was caught on a video dated September 26 admitting that the El-Sayed campaign still has a lot of work to do "to connect with the black community."

An MS NOW panel of pro-Israel Democrats similarly expressed skepticism of El-Sayed — with good reason. 

A former staffer for his campaign is under federal indictment in connection with anti-Semitic attacks, his family members have been linked to Islamic terrorist groups, and he infamously responded to the Hezbollah-inspired attack on Temple Israel in March by saying, "Hurt people hurt people."

"I can't vote for Abdul El-Sayed because, once again, he's going against something that's innately me," said one Jewish mother.

"I might go to Mike Rogers," said another.

Lansing Mayor Andy Schor, who is Jewish, indicated that the El-Sayed team has not made overtures for his support and that he may ultimately not vote for him. "If he doesn’t need me, he doesn’t need me," Schor stated, according to CNN.

Democrat Attorney General Dana Nessel, who is also Jewish, initially distanced herself from El-Sayed but ultimately endorsed him.

In the last week, Blaze News has received multiple text messages from Nonnegotiable Michigan, a group of Democrat-voting Jews in Michigan who launched a month ago in part to "call on El-Sayed and Democratic candidates to affirm baseline commitments to Jewish safety and identity."

"We've always shown up overwhelmingly for Democrats — but our support requires us to feel safe and valued in the party that has been our political home," read a message delivered Sunday.

Scholten and the El-Sayed campaign did not respond to requests for comment from Blaze News.

Greg Manz, senior communications director for the Michigan GOP, characterized El-Sayed as a "conman" who "has repeatedly brushed off concerns from black voters" even as he is being "bankrolled by elements tied to the Muslim Brotherhood."

"The exodus of Jewish and black Democrats from Conman Abdul El-Sayed's camp exposes his crumbling coalition," Manz said in a statement to Blaze News.

Apple News hid stories that reported on the weak financial condition of the Democratic National Committee (DNC) is ahead of the midterm elections, according to the Media Research Center.

Media Research Center (MRC) identified 78 stories about the DNC’s mounting debt, finding that none of them were promoted on Apple News’ top 20 stories from January 1 through September 28, according to the analysis, obtained by the New York Post.

Notably, September 28 marks just five weeks before the 2026 midterm elections — and nearly a year after the DNC disclosed that it is in millions of dollars in debt.

“Apple isn’t curating the news,” MRC President David Bozell said. “It’s running a high-tech protection racket for the political left.”

The MRC found that at least 14 stories about the DNC’s debt from outlets that Apple News typically promotes were also not featured, including USA Today, the Guardian, the New York Times, the Washington Post, the Wall Street Journal, and Politico.

“Our study found Apple News suppressing coverage of the Democratic Party’s fundraising woes while eagerly serving up stories damaging to Republicans,” Bozell told the Post, adding that stories promoted by the service can generate anywhere from 1 million to 20 million page views.

Interestingly, Apple News uses human editors to select many of the stories that appear on its platform — unlike Google News and Microsoft’s MSN, which depend heavily on algorithms to select and arrange stories.

Late last year, the DNC blamed its nearly $16 million debt on the ill-fated 2024 Biden-Harris campaign. From there, Kamala Harris’ failed 2024 presidential reportedly campaign spent around $1.5 billion.

By the end of it, the Democratic National Committee was left with $20.5 million in debt. then, in October 2025, the DNC took out a $15 million loan for gubernatorial elections.

The DNC rang in 2026 with $17.5 million in debt, according to a report by the New York Times. Meanwhile, the Republican National Committee (RNC) has $230 million in the bank and no debt.

“For years, the media lectured Americans about ‘dirty money in politics’ whenever Republicans had the fundraising advantage,” Bozell told the Post. “Now Democrats are facing a financial mess of their own making, and suddenly the story isn’t worth telling.”

As Breitbart News reported, the DNC’s financial woes have sparked calls to oust DNC Chairman Ken Martin, who has found himself increasingly isolated, throwing a phone at a junior aide’s desk in frustration.

Alana Mastrangelo-Wrask is a reporter for Breitbart News. You can follow her on Facebook and X at @ARmastrangelo, and on Instagram.
