news.title: Democrats' Blue Wave Could Miss New York
news.text: Democrats enter the final weeks of the 2026 midterms with favorable tailwinds as voters sour on President Donald Trump, but polls suggest the party may not be matching its national momentum in New York, the state that experienced the nation’s largest rightward shift in 2024. With less than four weeks until the November 3 midterm elections, Democrats are expanding their lead nationally and are working to expand the electoral battleground to compete in more conservative states like Alaska, Iowa, Kansas and Texas. But two recent surveys have produced underwhelming results for Democrats in New York, long seen as a major progressive stronghold, raising questions about whether the "blue wave” will manifest itself in the Empire State. As Democrats expand their lead on the national generic ballot, that has not translated into gains in New York, with recent polls showing Democrats up between 11 and 13 points in the state. The polls could signal a worrying trend for New York Democrats. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won the state by fewer than 13 points in 2024, down from former President Joe Biden’s 23-point victory in 2020. No other state saw a larger jump to the right in the most recent presidential race. The trend was driven by Trump’s inroads among Hispanic and Asian American voters, as well as more stagnant suburbs outside of New York City. That rightward shift also showed up further down the ballot, with Democrats winning the generic congressional vote by 15 points, down from 24 points in 2020, according to SplitTicket. Boris Heersink, a political science professor at Fordham University, told Newsweek that if Trump’s 2024 coalition lasted in New York, it could “produce an environment where a particularly appealing Republican could do well” in the state. But he also said that does not “seem to be the most likely outcome.” “I don't think the current polls suggest a long-term trend away from the Democrats. What I think is clear is that the era where Democrats were completely dominating New York in the 2010s is over,” he said. New York Polls Show Democrats Lagging National Gains Recent polling data suggest Democrats are struggling to rebuild their dominance in New York politics, even in a more favorable environment ahead of the midterm elections, though it could ultimately come down to how undecided voters break between now and November 3. These polls still give Democrats a statewide advantage. Democrats led Republicans on the generic ballot by only 13 points, 55 percent to 42 percent, in a new Marist University poll of New York registered voters. Meanwhile, in the gubernatorial race, Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul led her Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive, by only 11 points, 53 percent to 42 percent. The poll surveyed 1,361 registered voters from October 1 to 4 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. Just weeks earlier, a Siena University poll produced similarly concerning results for Democrats. It found Democrats leading the generic ballot by only 11 points, 51 percent to 40 percent, while Hochul was up only 9 points, 50 percent to 41 percent. The poll surveyed 1,144 likely voters from September 11 to 17, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.2 percentage points. However, a recent Quinnipiac University poll was a bit better for Hochul, showing her up 19 points, 58 percent to 39 percent. It polled 1,026 likely voters from September 17 to 20 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.1 percentage points. Historically, New York has shifted against Republican presidents. In 2018, Democrats won the generic ballot by 31 points in New York, a shift from a 22-point win in 2016. How New York Compares With National Polling At the same time, Democrats are in a strong position on the generic ballot. RealClearPolitics gives Democrats a 7.8-point lead in their aggregate, while Nate Silver showed Democrats up 9 points as of Wednesday. That marks a notable shift from 2024, when Republicans won the generic ballot by 2.7 points. Polling shifts have been driven by a decline in Trump’s approval rating. Historically, when the president is unpopular ahead of the midterms, his party tends to lose seats in the House and Senate. Democrats have sought to make the midterms a referendum on Trump as he faces voter backlash over the economy, cost of living and high gas prices amid the Iran war. But midterm shifts are not always even, and some polling suggests other Democratic states like Massachusetts and Oregon are also not seeing significant leftward trends this year. Meanwhile, races in states like Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas, which backed Trump by double digits in 2024, appear more competitive. New York voters have a “long-standing and deep frustration” with state-level politics, which may help explain why polls show the state is closer than expected in the midterms, Grant Davis Reeher, a political science professor at Syracuse University, told Newsweek. “Affordability here is just as likely to focus on the state’s high taxes and spending as on the price of gas and eggs,” he said. “That provides avenues for Republicans to make a case, at least, even in a very blue state. In addition, most of the Republicans that are left in office, or that are running, are more moderate than the typical Republican, and especially the MAGA Republican.” What This Means for Key Midterm Races Hochul remains the favorite to win reelection, as she has not trailed a single public poll. The Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball both consider the race to be solid or safe for Democrats. New York has some important congressional races. In New York’s 3rd District, Democratic Representative Tom Suozzi is facing a challenge from Republican State Assemblymember Mike LePetri. Democrats are also hoping to flip New York’s 17th District, a Harris-won seat held by GOP Representative Mike Lawler. Democrats are running Cait Conley in that race. These are two seats that could determine whether Democrats or Republicans will control the House of Representatives after the midterms. Reeher said he doubts that Democrats will lose any seats at the federal level in New York. “At the state and local level, you might see some upsets, if local issues can combine with a lesser blue wave at the top of the ticket to produce the right formula,” Reeher said. Ciro Riccardi, a spokesperson for Lawler’s campaign, pointed to Hochul as a vulnerability for New York Democrats. "She is deeply underwater with independents and in the suburbs thanks to her policies: sanctuary laws that protect criminals, sky-high taxes, and non-stop utility bill increases approved by her PSC,” Riccardi said. Conley’s “refusal to campaign publicly with Hochul tells you everything you need to know about Hochul’s impact on down ballot races,” he said. In a statement to Newsweek, the LePetri campaign said that “all politics are local” and that Democrats in New York “no longer work for the people.” “Taxin’ Tom Suozzi voted against the largest working families tax cut in history and voted to allow men in girls sports. Meanwhile Horrible Hochul is driving up utility costs and driving out businesses and young people. The last piece of the ‘Terrible Trifecta’ is Zohran ‘Commie’ Mamdani whose disastrous socialist policies are right here in NY-03 in northeast Queens and the DSA is pledging to bring more of it to Nassau County,” the statement reads. A Hochul campaign spokesperson told Newsweek that the governor is “continuing to build momentum as we near Election Day." “Bruce Blakeman has spent his failing campaign tying himself to an unpopular Trump, saying high gas prices aren’t a ‘New York issue,’ the governor’s moratorium on data centers is ‘crazy,’ and that ICE has done a ‘very, very good job,’” the spokesperson said. Newsweek also reached out to the Blakeman, Conley and Suozzi campaigns for comment. Progressives Surge in New York City—Is That Alienating Moderates? Despite Republicans making some inroads in the Empire State, New York City has become a progressive stronghold over the past few years, defined by Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s victory in the 2025 race against former Governor Andrew Cuomo and Republican Curtis Sliwa. In 2026, progressives, including Democratic socialists, gained ground in New York. Candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila-Chevalier, along with progressive Brad Lander, won Democratic primaries in House races. Avila-Chevalier and Lander unseated more moderate incumbents, major victories for the left. The DSA also won major victories in local races, as well, and have become a power player in New York politics. Some Democrats, however, have raised concerns that DSA’s rise could alienate more moderate Democrats and independents, even in cases where Democratic candidates are more moderate, such as Hochul, Suozzi or Conley. Suozzi warned that there is “little support” for their ideas in remarks to Fox News Digital in August. “Much like the Republicans have had to deal with the Freedom Caucus, the Democrats are going to have to deal with this group,” Suozzi told the outlet. Heersink said it is “very difficult” to know if the progressive surge is actually harming other Democrats. “Moderate Democrats always have a tendency to blame any underperformance on people in their party pushing them to the left. There may very well be some voters who are traditionally Democrats who do not like Mamdani and what he represents,” he said. “But there's also the potential counter-side that the DSA wing of the party is able to bring out younger voters.” A plurality of New Yorkers, 43 percent, view DSA unfavorably, compared to just 29 percent who view it favorably, according to the Quinnipiac poll. Those numbers are even lower outside of the city. In the suburbs, 26 percent of voters view DSA favorably, compared with 23 percent upstate, the poll found. What Happens Next How New York votes in November, as well as in the 2028 election, will be watched as a critical gauge of the state’s political future. Key metrics to watch could include the outcome in suburban regions on Long Island and in the Hudson River Valley, as well as how Hispanic and Asian American neighborhoods in New York City vote. As for New York's political future, the state is unlikely to be competitive in 2028, Reeher said. “I have a hard time imagining New York to be in serious play at the presidential level anytime soon,” he said. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Sam Wilson.
news.summary: New York swung to the right more than any state in 2024. Now, polls show Democrats' momentum may be trailing in the Empire State.
news.author: Andrew Stanton

news.title: Trump Voters Back Abdul El-Sayed 5 to 1 in Live TV Panel Poll
news.text: A televised MSNOW panel of 10 Trump voters favored Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed over Republican Mike Rogers. El-Sayed is running against Rogers in a closely watched midterm race considered a key battleground, as the Democrats bid to take control of the Senate this November. Six participants said they had decided how they would vote in the race. Five raised their hands for El-Sayed, while one backed Rogers. The remaining four in the small sample were undecided, although one said she leaned “heavily” toward Rogers. If all four undecided voters ultimately supported Rogers, the panel would have been evenly divided, with five voters backing each candidate. Newsweek reached out to El-Sayed and Rogers’ campaigns for comment, via email and online contact form, respectively, on Wednesday. MSNOW’s Elise Jordan also asked those backing El-Sayed how firmly they had settled on their choice. “Pretty firm,” responded one. “I’m about 90 percent,” said another, adding: “If I don’t vote for him, I’m not voting.” The panelists were also asked what changes they had hoped Trump would bring about when they voted for him in 2024. “I think a lot of people looked at his 2016 win and how much better the country was before [COVID-19], and hoped that it would replicate that,” one responded. “To me it doesn’t seem like it has.” El-Sayed to Campaign with Obama in Michigan El-Sayed announced on Monday that former President Barack Obama would campaign alongside him in Detroit later this month. “It is my honor and privilege to announce that [Obama] is joining us on the trail in Detroit on Saturday, October 24,” El-Sayed wrote on X. Former Vice President Kamala Harris made a joint appearance with El-Sayed last month. Michigan Senate Race: Latest Polls Three recent Michigan polls placed El-Sayed just ahead of Rogers in a tight Senate race. A Quantus Insights survey of 762 likely voters published Wednesday placed El-Sayed at 47.6 percent and Rogers at 46.5 percent. The poll had a margin of error of approximately plus or minus 7.8 points. A YouGov poll conducted between September 22 and October 4 among 3,949 likely voters put El-Sayed at 49 percent and Rogers at 48 percent. This survey had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. Meanwhile, polling conducted by Mitchell Research and Communications for CBS News Detroit placed El-Sayed at 45.6 percent and Rogers at 41.4 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points and was conducted among more than 680 likely voters. Trump’s Approval in Michigan As Newsweek reported on Wednesday, recent polling data from research firm Civiqs showed President Donald Trump’s approval stood at -26 points in the key battleground state, which backed Trump by less than 2 points in 2024. El-Sayed’s Past Citizenship Remarks The Washington Free Beacon reported on Monday that video from a 2016 medical conference in Detroit showed Abdul El-Sayed saying he carried dual citizenship in the U.S. and Egypt. The outlet said the footage was the second known instance in which El-Sayed had described himself as a dual citizen, after it previously reported that a 2014 academic résumé listed him as a citizen of both countries. His campaign reportedly previously told the Free Beacon that El-Sayed had never held dual citizenship and had mistakenly believed otherwise based on information passed down by relatives. The outlet said his campaign did not respond to questions about the reported 2016 remarks. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Matthew Cannon and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed led Republican Mike Rogers among Trump voters in a televised MSNOW panel.
news.author: Joe Edwards

news.title: Trump makes late Nobel Prize pitch: ‘Not bragging ... but I settled eight wars’
news.text:
Donald Trump re-issued his call for the Nobel Prize committee to award him with the Nobel Peace Prize on Wednesday as he leaned back into talk of his peacemaking efforts.

Those peacemaking efforts, he says, are ongoing and will soon include “another one” — even though there’s no signs yet of meaningful progress in talks between the U.S. and Iran regarding another ceasefire.

The president spoke to reporters at an announcement on his “Trump accounts” for children, after returning to Washington from a spree of campaign appearances across the country.

“I’ve done stuff that nobody else has ever done. I’m not bragging, I’m just telling you the facts,” the president told reporters on Wednesday. “No president has probably ever settled any wars. I settled 8 wars."

He then went after his predecessor, Barack Obama, whom he accused of not knowing why he’d received the 2009 Peace prize. The foundation in charge of awarding the prize gave the 2009 peace prize to Obama, then less than a year into his presidency, for his diplomatic efforts to reestablish ties with the Muslim world after nearly a decade of warfare in Iraq and Afghanistan led to a perception held by some that America was at war with the entire Muslim world.

The 47th president said on Wednesday that he was more deserving of the prize than Obama.

“Look, Obama got it, and he didn’t do anything-- he still doesn’t know what he got it for,” said Trump. “He got it when he was elected, right? Right at the beginning.”

“Whether I get it or not, I have done far more [than anyone else],” the president said.

The president frequently cites the “eight wars” statistic as a reference for his supposed peacemaking abilities, but the figure is not true. Several of the “wars” on Trump’s list were not wars at all, such as disagreements between Serbia and Kosovo which never escalated to real armed conflict during either of Trump’s two presidencies. Another one of the eight is the conflict between Iran and Israel, which very much remains ongoing as part of a three-way conflict also now involving the U.S. — that conflict has been ongoing for nearly eight months.

The Iran conflict has largely shattered Trump’s image as a steward of global affairs in the minds of his own supporters, who embraced that depiction of the president during his 2024 campaign for a second term as he hammered Joe Biden and Kamala Harris over Israel’s war against Gaza and the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, both of which he pledged to end.

A year and a half after coming to power, Trump has made little to no progress in his efforts to negotiate an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine. A ceasefire exists in the Gaza Strip, where the majority of fighting has died down, but most Gazans remain in appalling conditions with much of the region’s infrastructure and housing destroyed. Israeli strikes continue to be carried out on camps of refugees, with continued civilian casualties.

The president’s touting of his diplomatic credentials also ignore one truth about his 2024 campaign: his promise to stop getting the U.S. into endless wars with murky objectives. His critics, both within and outside of the Republican Party, now accuse him of doing just that as the war in Iran has shifted from an effort to dislodge the Iranian government and take control of its remaining nuclear materials to ending disruptions over shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Obama has long been a fixation of Trump’s, however, and the president attacks him nearly as frequently as he attacks Biden, who defeated him in the 2020 election. On Wednesday, he warned that his allies wanted to see the Justice Department wielded against Obama, Biden and Hillary Clinton, but claimed that he was respecting the sanctity of his office by declining.

"I could've done very bad things to Hillary Clinton. I could've done very very bad things to Joe Biden. I could've done very bad things to Barack Hussein Obama,” said Trump.

As he departed the White House for a campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas, the president reiterated his confusing claim that the war in Iran was already “won”, but not yet “over”.

“It's a war that's been won from the standpoint of what we have to do. We have to get rid of-- no nuclear weapons for, as you know, for Iran,” said the president. “We've taken away their nuclear power. If they would have had nuclear power, you would have had problems like you've never had before. So we did this for that reason. We've essentially accomplished that. Their military is now wiped out. Their whole country right now is wiped out. It'll be over very quickly. And when it does, and when it does, oil prices will come tumbling down.”
news.author: John Bowden

news.title: El-Sayed Is Aiming To Unify Michigan. There's One Unknown That Could Cost Him.
news.text:
WARREN, Mich. — Democrats are a little less worried about Abdul El-Sayed these days, even if they still can’t stop arguing about him.

The progressive Senate candidate, who won an $81 million battle against moderate Rep. Haley Stevens to claim the party’s nomination for U.S. Senate in August, spent months fighting concerns about his electability and whether he could unite a splintered Democratic Party. 

But as he campaigned with the more moderate Sen. Elissa Slotkin and held town halls in a majority-Black city and a quintessential swing county over the weekend, the uber-confident El-Sayed’s certainty of victory seemed to have spread to the rest of his party. Still, loud holdouts remain, and concerns persist about GOP candidate Mike Rogers’ spending advantages in the state, with a media-buying source saying Republicans are expected to outspend Democrats by more than $20 million in the final weeks of the contest.

Asked if he was concerned about party unity, El-Sayed responded: “Of course.” But in an interview, he made clear his goal was broader.

“My goal is to unite the state around this campaign,” he told HuffPost. “We all understand, even if we had our differences in the primary, that what we’re up against is a lot worse than anything that divided us.”

And while El-Sayed’s progressive policies — including his support for “Medicare for All” and opposition to aid to Israel — defined much of his primary campaign, his efforts against Rogers have largely been in step with other Democratic campaigns, relentlessly focused on corruption, affordability and the link between the two.

Polling indicates the efforts are working, with El-Sayed consistently holding a slight lead over Rogers. He’s also continuing to get backup from national party figures: After former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned for him in September, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani appeared at a fundraiser for him on Monday, just hours after President Barack Obama announced a campaign event for later this month.

And while Rogers’ campaign has made a significant show of reaching out to Democrats, polling gives little indication there are many defectors: a New York Times survey found just 3% of Democrats and 5% of those who backed Harris in 2024 were voting for the Republican, while El-Sayed was picking up 8% of those who supported Trump two years ago and dominating among those who didn’t cast a ballot.

This has led some of El-Sayed’s earlier detractors to admit his relative strengths: The Never-Trump Republican pollster Sarah Longwell marveled at his ability to win over Trump voters in a recent piece, and Center for American Progress President Neera Tanden — arguably Stevens’ biggest online booster — praised El-Sayed’s ability to unite the party during a Monday night appearance on CNN. 

At the same time, the symbolism of a potential El-Sayed win, highlighted by Ocasio-Cortez’s prediction at Monday’s fundraiser that his victory would “break open the entire political calculus in America,” essentially guarantees his candidacy will remain a political football in the never-ending back-and-forth between the party’s progressive and moderate wings. 

Rogers’ campaign did not respond to repeated requests for comment.

The enthusiasm for El-Sayed among some Michiganders was apparent standing in the back of a Flint, Michigan, church on Saturday, where supporters carrying signs and wearing football jerseys emblazoned with his name crammed into the sanctuary. The candidate, wearing a black, long-sleeve shirt under a suit jacket that he quickly shed as he took the stage, stayed issues-focused as he answered questions about Social Security, the cost of living and corruption in the Trump administration.

“A lot of the pundits — you know — the people on TV who are smarter than the rest of us, they’re always like, ‘he can’t win,’” El-Sayed told one supporter. “It’s like they think that people out here are running around thinking, ‘Where do I fit on the left-right spectrum? Is he a little bit too far to the left for me?’ I think most people are running around thinking, ‘How am I going to afford my rent, my car, my insurance and my groceries?’”

Speaking to HuffPost in an interview following the event, El-Sayed reiterated that he thought the popular momentum was behind him. “We know that the Trump agenda is devastating Michiganders,” he said. “I hear that from everywhere, and everybody that I talk to. You see the excitement here on the ground.”

Later that day, El-Sayed made another stop at the carpenters’ union banquet hall in Warren, Detroit’s largest suburb and part of Macomb County, which decidedly backed President Donald Trump in the 2024 election. It was an event characterized by firsts — El-Sayed’s campaign had never before traveled to Warren, and he had never directly campaigned alongside Slotkin.

“We don’t agree on everything, and that’s OK,” said Slotkin. “We agree on the things that are really important: putting a check on this man in the White House who is trying to tell us America is over.”

And the sitting Michigan senator poured cold water on discussions about political rifts within her party. “The debate of moderate versus progressive is not the real debate,” she told the crowd. “The real debate among Democrats right now is fight versus flight. I need someone who is with me on ‘team fight.’”

The crowd in Warren, which filled the banquet hall to capacity, showed no signs of backing down from El-Sayed. Many voters felt his message spoke directly to them.

“We’re sick of the bullshit,” said Eric Ciaglo, a 75-year-old from Harrison, Michigan, who attended the event with his wife. “The corruption. It’s right in our face. All these years, I’ve never seen such corruption and bullshit ... and people accepting it.”

And state Rep. Mai Xiong, a Democrat who represents parts of Warren, said she thought El-Sayed was within striking distance in Macomb County, which had gone for Trump in the past three presidential elections. 

“They come here because they know that the pathway to winning runs through this community,” Xiong said, adding that she “100%” thought El-Sayed could flip the county. “To know that the Abdul campaign is hearing that and understanding the importance of picking up these votes here — that’s how we’re gonna win.” 

But behind the rosy atmosphere of El-Sayed’s campaign events, where most attendees appear to have made up their minds about casting their votes in November, there lies an undercurrent of tension, particularly among Black voters in the Detroit area who, according to state political leaders, are still wary of the Democrat after largely backing Stevens in the primary.

“I think there needs to be more solidarity with Black people,” said Kimberly Fisher, a small business owner running to represent parts of Detroit and Warren in the Michigan legislature. “Detroit is the Blackest city in the country, and there’s been no engagement.”

Anyone with worries about support for El-Sayed in Michigan’s Black communities would not have been placated by the crowds at his campaign events in Warren and Flint. Though the latter city’s population is 56% Black, the crowd gathered at St. Michael’s Conference Center was mostly white.

Fisher, who has a longstanding relationship with El-Sayed and supports his campaign, told HuffPost in an interview she thought the candidate had a “passion” for the Black community in Detroit — pointing to his work expanding a municipal financial aid program for childcare and his support following a recent tornado in the area — but that she hadn’t seen that same passion on the campaign trail.

And it might be too late for him to salvage those votes, warned Fisher, who previously raised her concerns directly with El-Sayed during a town hall meeting last month. At the time, El Sayed said he wanted to “bring communities together” as the son of an immigrant who understood “the debt of gratitude I owe to Black communities who advocated for the right of my dad to even immigrate here in the first place.” 

“We’re talking months and months of missed opportunities,” Fisher said. “We’re talking about ignoring a community that is a large part of your voter base.”

Fisher said lingering tensions between Black and Arab communities are still hurting El-Sayed, with many Black people in Detroit feeling the Arab American community “looks down” on them. 

Many of the state’s Jewish voters, too, continue to find El-Sayed’s opposition to aid to Israel and belief that the country is committing a genocide in Gaza to be unacceptable. 

But while Rogers has focused extensively on El-Sayed’s foreign policy positions, there’s little indication it’s hurting the Democrat: Voters in the Times survey are split on who they trust more to handle the Israel-Palestine conflict, but say they would prefer a candidate who opposes aid to Israel by a 38% to 29% margin over one who supports it.
news.author: Benjamin S. Weiss

news.title: Michigan's Mike Rogers Seizes on October 7 Anniversary to Attack El-Sayed
news.text: Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers used the third anniversary of the October 7 Hamas attacks in Israel to attack Democratic rival Abdul El-Sayed, accusing him of spreading antisemitism and sympathizing with terrorists. In a statement Wednesday, Rogers accused El-Sayed of fundraising off October 7, campaigning with progressive commentator Hasan Piker and appearing to sympathize with the attacker who targeted Temple Israel in Michigan earlier this year. "At a time when we especially need to turn the temperature down and stand alongside our Jewish friends and neighbors, he only spreads antisemitism and incites more violence," Rogers said. The attack is part of Rogers' broader effort to make El-Sayed's views on Israel, Hamas and antisemitism a central issue in the closely watched Michigan Senate race, where Rogers has trailed in polling in the weeks leading up to the November 3 election. El-Sayed and his campaign have not yet commented on the anniversary as of Wednesday morning. Newsweek reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for comment Wednesday. Antisemitism Has Shadowed the Race Since the Primary El-Sayed, who would become the first Muslim U.S. senator if elected, has been an outspoken critic of Israel's war in Gaza, which he has described as a genocide, and has called for ending U.S. military aid to Israel. Rogers' Wednesday attack also revived a controversy from last year's anniversary. On October 7, 2025, El-Sayed's campaign, which was still in the primary race at the time, sent supporters a fundraising email criticizing Israel's ground invasion of Gaza while making no mention of the Hamas attack that preceded it. A campaign spokesperson said the email "mistakenly went out" the day before. Michigan state Senator Mallory McMorrow, then one of El-Sayed's primary rivals, called it "beyond tone deaf." Scrutiny grew over the spring, when El-Sayed rallied at the University of Michigan and Michigan State University with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker, who had called Orthodox Jews "inbred" and described Zionism as a "mental illness." Michigan Representative Haley Stevens, a Democrat and El-Sayed's rival for the Democratic nomination at the time, accused him of "choosing to campaign with someone who has a history of antisemitic rhetoric." El-Sayed later put distance between himself and Piker. Israel also dominated the money in the Democratic primary. The United Democracy Project, AIPAC's largest super PAC, spent a record $30.6 million in this race backing Stevens. El-Sayed made AIPAC and the tens of millions of dollars spent to support Stevens a centerpiece of his campaign, casting the contest as "the many versus the money." Stevens, in turn, said El-Sayed wants to "blame all of your problems on Jewish Americans." On the morning of October 7, 2023, Hamas militants fired several thousand rockets into Israel and thousands of militants attacked through holes blown in the border fence or with boats or motorized paragliders. Some 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostage. Israel responded with a military offensive that has killed over 74,000 Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, according to local health authorities cited by the Associated Press, left the territory in ruins and sparked an ongoing humanitarian catastrophe. Polls Show a Tight Race in Michigan Rogers' attack comes as recent polls show El-Sayed holding a narrow edge, with several of the latest surveys putting the race within a single point. A Quantus Insights poll conducted October 5 to 6 found El-Sayed leading Rogers 48 percent to 47 percent among 744 likely voters. A YouGov survey of 3,947 likely voters, taken September 22 to October 4, showed the same 1-point margin, 49 percent to 48 percent. A Fox News poll, conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research from September 24 to 28, also had El-Sayed up by a point, 50 percent to 49 percent among 1,028 likely voters. Trafalgar Group, a Republican-leaning firm, found him ahead 47 percent to 45 percent among 1,085 likely voters in a survey taken September 28 to 30. Other polls have given El-Sayed more breathing room. news.title: Can $1 billion power Republicans to victory in the US midterm elections?
news.text: WASHINGTON: Republicans are entering the final month of the midterm campaign increasingly anxious that the $1 billion at their disposal may not be enough to fend off sweeping losses as the party reckons with President Donald Trump's unpopularity, persistent cost concerns and the fallout from the war in Iran.The cash advantage, spread out across a half-dozen groups, is driven largely by the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc., which had nearly $416 million in cash on hand at the end of August and began stepping up its spending on critical races in September.But that money may have come too late, forcing the president's group to pay much higher rates because of the shrinking availability of air time. Four Republican Senate campaign officials said groups that reserved advertising time last spring paid much lower rates than MAGA Inc. and its affiliated groups.Instead, by waiting until September, Trump-connected organizations are sometimes paying more than five times what they would have spent if they acted earlier.A representative of MAGA Inc. familiar with the group's strategy said its spending has allowed Republicans to keep races more competitive than they would have been otherwise. In some cases, the group has been the only one on the air criticizing Democratic candidates.The MAGA Inc. representative and the Republican Senate campaign officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal strategy.The challenge is acute in places like Texas, where Trump will travel on Wednesday for the second time in a week to stump for Republican Ken Paxton's Senate campaign. The state hasn't elected a Democratic senator since 1988, yet MAGA Inc. has spent more than $22 million in the past month, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact.Another group, Texas PAC, which is aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, has spent more than $83 million on advertising in the past month, an extraordinary amount to protect what's normally a safe Republican seat.One of those advertisements, which featured Paxton's estranged wife saying she's supporting the full Republican ticket, aired across the United States last weekend during a football game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Houston Texans.Candidates are charged a lower advertising rate than outside groups, so the late infusion of super PAC cash has come at a steep price.MAGA Inc., which is running ads primarily on streaming services, has been charged roughly $894 per airing, according to AdImpact, while Texas PAC has been charged roughly $809 for a mix of broadcast and streaming. That compares with about $290 for Democratic nominee James Talarico's campaign, also on broadcast and streaming.Those averages mask some of the more glaring disparities. For example, during a football game last month, Texas PAC was charged $450,000 to air a single spot in the Austin market. Talarico's campaign paid $50,000 for a spot during the same game in the same market, according to AdImpact..Elections are a referendum on the power of moneyThe 2026 campaign is shaping up as a referendum on the power of money in American politics. Democrats freely acknowledge their disadvantage, relying instead on anti-Trump sentiment among voters and targeted messaging on issues like corruption. Some Republicans, meanwhile, are open about the challenge of trying to spend their way out of a tough campaign at this late stage.Neil Newhouse, a longtime Republican pollster, echoed concerns that his party was deploying its cash too late."After the votes are counted, I think we're going to find the most effective advertising in terms of communicating message and moving voters and poll numbers, the most effective time was advertising that happened well before Labor Day, not after it," he said. "A million dollars of advertising in October is a drop in the bucket."Thune's group began pulling back in North Carolina last week, a sign of the party's challenge in the Senate race there. The state's outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis has been increasingly vocal about his party's vulnerabilities and recently said that, even with a strong cash advantage, "in the last month, you pretty much have to place your bets.""If we have endless resources, then we should spend endlessly in every state," he said. "Absent endless resources, you've got to make data-driven decisions about where you can win."The midterms mark the first national election since the Supreme Court in June erased limits on how much political parties can spend in coordination with candidates for Congress and president, injecting even more money into a political system already awash in cash.Money alone doesn't translate into victoryThere's plenty of evidence that money alone doesn't translate into victory.Democrat Kamala Harris entered the final stretch of the 2024 campaign with significantly more money than Trump but went on to lose every critical swing state and the White House. Elon Musk's $25 million didn't lift his preferred candidate to a Wisconsin Supreme Court seat last year. And Tom Steyer didn't advance to the general election in the California governor's race despite pumping $216 million of his own money into the campaign.The $1 billion that Republicans have amassed compares with roughly $579 million held by a comparable collection of major Democratic groups.Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said his party is facing an "obscene" amount of spending that could swamp them in the midterms."We're never going to have as much money as them," he said in an interview. "I sum up the election in this sentence: Can a massive Republican advantage in money beat a massive Democratic advantage in better candidates and political climate? I bet it can't."In addition to Texas, Democrats have mounted competitive Senate campaigns in states like Ohio, Maine, Iowa and Michigan. A similar dynamic has emerged in governors' races from Florida and Georgia to Wisconsin, Ohio and Nevada.Former President Barack Obama is stepping up his involvement in the midterms and will headline a fundraiser for Senate candidates on Wednesday.In the House, Democrats are growing so confident they can retake the majority that they're expanding their targets deeper into traditionally Republican districts in Arkansas and Tennessee. But a lack of money could limit their gains."We absolutely need to spend enough to get our message out," said Rep. Suzan DelBene of Washington, who chairs the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. "And district by district, we are."Trump turns to his bond with supportersFrom his earliest days as an unlikely political figure, Trump has consistently overcome expectations. Facing daunting prospects heading into the final weeks of his last midterm, he's betting he can again outwit political gravity, relying in large part on the deep bond he's built with supporters.He has stepped up his campaign rallies in recent weeks, traveling to deep red territory to galvanize the party faithful. At events like the one this past weekend in Vandalia, Ohio, the crowd was enthusiastic and cheered at the lines that have become Trump staples over the years, particularly when he dips into profanity. The high school gymnasium that held the event was packed, though crowds began emptying out about halfway through the 90-minute rally.In the closing minutes of a speech Monday in Grand Island, Nebraska, the president revived his plea that supporters who have stood so fervently by him pretend as if he is on the ballot one more time."In a true way, I am running," he said. "We have to keep it going.".Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Judge Lets Maryland’s Glock Ban Stand
news.text:
A federal judge in Maryland refused to block the state’s ban on Glock pistols Monday, arguing it was “consistent with restrictions on excessively dangerous weapons.”

Democratic Maryland Gov. Wes Moore signed legislation in May that banned the sale of Glock pistols by labeling them “machinegun convertible pistols,” one of a handful of states targeting the popular semiautomatic pistol over illegal modifications. United States Senior District Judge Richard D. Bennett, a George W. Bush appointee, issued his written opinion Monday, making an earlier bench ruling allowing the ban to take effect official. (RELATED: Gun Rights Groups Slap Blue State’s Glock Ban With New Court Filing)

“The Court finds that Plaintiffs have failed to demonstrate a clear likelihood of success on the merits. Plaintiffs have demonstrated that SB 334 covers conduct within the Second Amendment’s plain text,” Bennett wrote. “However, Plaintiffs have failed to demonstrate a likelihood of success at Bruen’s Step 2. Defendants have introduced well-documented evidence that SB 334 fits within the country’s historic tradition of regulating technologically advanced weapons which have the ‘potential for widespread criminal abuse or [an] unreasonable capacity to inflict casualties.’”

FPC LEGAL UPDATE: A Maryland federal judge today denied our motion for a preliminary injunction against the state’s Glock ban, saying that the law "is a commensurate response [] to today’s unrelenting tide of mass shootings and gun violence." https://t.co/yg6HnfqOCj https://t.co/lHw0EvYjNo— Firearms Policy Coalition (@gunpolicy) October 5, 2026

Maryland attorneys told a federal court in August that the state could ban Glock pistols despite their popularity among Americans, even though the landmark 2008 Heller decision invalidated Washington, D.C.’s ban on handguns on the grounds that firearms that were commonly used for lawful purposes could not be banned due to the Second Amendment.

“We were disappointed that the court denied our request for preliminary injunction and allowed Maryland’s unconstitutional Glock ban to take effect,” Second Amendment Foundation (SAF) Senior Director of Litigation Bill Sack told the Daily Caller News Foundation. “The opinion makes a number of analytical errors that are unfortunately consistent with the errors made by the Fourth Circuit on similar issues. We are confident that the appeal process and ultimately the Supreme Court will strike this law down.”

On Sept. 30, United States District Judge Kari A. Dooley of the District of Connecticut, a Trump appointee, said that Connecticut’s ban on Glock pistols failed the testing process established by the Supreme Court’s decision in New York State Rifle and Pistol Association v. Bruen.

Under the Supreme Court’s rulings in Heller and Bruen, firearms in common use for lawful purposes fall under the Second Amendment’s protection. Glock pistols are among the most popular in the United States, regularly appearing in lists of the most-sold firearms compiled by outlets like Guns and Guns and Ammo magazine.

In addition to being popular among law-abiding citizens, Glock pistols are also used by numerous law enforcement agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), which has issued versions of the handgun to its agents since 1997. Former Vice President Kamala Harris boasted on multiple occasions about owning a Glock pistol she acquired for personal protection.

Under current federal law, it is illegal to possess or manufacture a fully-automatic firearm that is not registered or authorized under the provisions of the National Firearms Act. The penalty for violating the NFA is ten years in federal prison.

news.title: Mid-Day Digest — October 7, 2026
news.text:
“Lord, I was born a ramblin’ man,” sang the Allman Brothers Band back in 1973. If anyone can identify with that, it’s Donald Trump.

President Ramblin’ Man struck again on Monday night at a rally in Grand Island, Nebraska. Here’s the relevant portion of Trump’s remarks from Roll Call’s transcript, in which he opined about Iran, high oil prices, nuclear weapons, Los Angeles, and San Diego:

But I want, I wanna see, I wanna see a tremendous victory. You wanna see a tremendous victory, because it verifies all the things we did. And again, remember, with the word, it’s just artificial, it’s a little bit high. It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe.They can take out a city. Let them take, let it, let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That’s, this is a very small price to pay, and it’s gonna be over very soon. It’s essentially almost over with. And they might keep going a little long, you know? They always say they have a big threshold for pain.They need it, let me tell you. They need it. But it’s gonna end very soon, and it’ll end one way or the other, and your gas and your gasoline and all of the things. And don’t forget, we also took on a country known as Venezuela. They never talk about that. They never talk about Venezuela. And we’re taking in hundreds of millions of barrels of oil every week.We’re pouring oil. We’re pouring oil into this country like nobody’s ever seen before.

The New York Times notes, “The audience cheered when he said ‘let them take out Los Angeles; let them take out San Diego,’ and the moment instantly went viral.” The Times isn’t wrong that some in the crowd cheered, though it was nowhere near the whole audience. The story has the video, so judge for yourself. The cheering is, to put it mildly, unfortunate. I’m no fan of LA or San Diego or anywhere else in the Democrat-run People’s Republic of California (go Braves, go Brewers), but cheering for even the vague idea of America’s enemies taking out an American city just shouldn’t happen.

Neither should an American president be so careless with his words, but that’s breaking news from 2017. This is vintage Trump — entertain a crowd with his Ramblin’ Man routine to make his black-and-white divide between how terrible his opponents are and how great he is. Some people love him for it. Others are suffering Trump fatigue.

But for the love of Pete, as the context about oil, Venezuela, and so forth makes obvious, everyone should know that Trump did not mean Iran should take out LA and San Diego.

Yet that’s exactly what Democrats accused him of saying.

“After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California,” California Democrat Governor Gavin Newsom posted on X, “Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego. He is deranged and dangerous.” Elsewhere, he called the president’s comments “treasonous.”

Newsom’s press office then posted, “Let’s be clear: The President is advocating for an attack on 10+ million U.S. residents in two of America’s largest cities.”

Kamala Harris’s “Headquarters” Bluesky account posted, “Trump on Iran: Let ’em take out Los Angeles and San Diego, it’s a small price to pay.”

LA Mayor Karen Bass, who let her city burn while she traveled to Africa last year, was “just shocked” by Trump’s comments and huffed, “It would really be helpful to our city if you would apologize.”

San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria chimed in, too. “San Diego is not collateral damage,” Gloria wrote on X. “We are not expendable. And we are never a ‘small price to pay.’ Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.”

Other Democrats piled on, too, but give me a break. Even the leftists at FactCheck.org get it.

Democrats know full well that Trump’s point, however buried in the word salad, was that high gas prices are a small price to pay to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon with which to take out an American city.

It’s that simple. Why can’t Trump say it that clearly? I have no idea, but Democrats and anyone in the media who amplified it are reprehensible for distorting his comments.

Trump’s military action against Iran is meant to protect America. One terrorist on an Israeli flight nearly did terrible damage. One terrorist with an Iranian nuke could do unthinkably worse.

Republican Congressman Darrell Issa is among those who understand this. “For five decades,” he said, “Americans on American soil have shed blood and lost their lives at the hands of Iran and its terrorist proxies. Where the Obama and Biden Administrations appeased Tehran, paid them billions in bribes, and put them on a glide path to having nuclear weapons, President Trump has taken historic and concrete action to eliminate the nuclear threat, protect every inch of our homeland, and ensure Iran never threatens America or her allies ever again.”

Maybe “Democrats don’t believe the polls,” wonders The Wall Street Journal’s James Freeman. “The leadership of the Democratic Party is so confident of success in November’s elections that they’ve launched an all-hands-on-social-media effort to promote an unbelievable characterization of President Donald Trump’s remarks,” he wrote. “This is not the behavior of people who think they are coasting to victory.”

He may have a point. Yes, Trump rambles and it can be hard to follow, but he clearly was not saying what Democrats accuse him of saying. If they’re so desperate to regain the levers of power in Congress that they’re willing to lie so egregiously about something so simple, what else are they lying about to win an election?

news.title: Why Paramount-Warner merger has sparked fears about press freedom  | Barbados Gazette – Barbados &
news.text:
Paramount Skydance has completed its takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, bringing CNN and CBS News under the same corporate ownership, in a deal that has raised concerns about editorial independence and freedom of speech.

The acquisition, worth about $110bn including debt, combines two of Hollywood’s biggest studios after months of legal challenges lodged by state attorneys general and unions.

The new company, Skydance Corporation, brings together HBO, CBS, Nickelodeon, Showtime, Comedy Central, DC Studios and Food Network, alongside streaming services Paramount plus and HBO Max.

But its control of two major US news organisations has drawn particular scrutiny. David Ellison, Skydance’s chairman and chief executive, has promised to preserve their editorial independence, but his father, Oracle cofounder Larry Ellison is a major financial backer of the deal, and has previously donated funds to US President Donald Trump and Israel.

Asked about the takeover on Tuesday, Trump welcomed it. “They’re terrific people, and it’s going to be a great company,” he said.

Why was the merger challenged?

The takeover faced initial opposition from Hollywood workers, politicians and state prosecutors concerned about the mounting concentration of power in an industry already dominated by a handful of companies.

Netflix initially reached an agreement to buy part of Warner Bros Discovery. Paramount then launched a competing bid, prompting a bidding war before Netflix walked away.

A California-led coalition of 12 state attorneys general sued to block the deal, saying that it would reduce competition and raise prices. The Writers Guild of America brought a separate challenge.

Both cases were settled in September when Paramount agreed to commitments relating to film production, support for displaced workers and protections for the news networks, including the creation of a new editorial independence board.

But the settlement did not end opposition to the deal. “This merger will stifle creativity, weaken free speech and cost people their jobs,” actor and activist Mark Ruffalo has said.

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren linked the takeover to Trump’s efforts to restrict media access. “As Trump tries to ban CNN from the White House, it would be a massive mistake to cave on the Paramount merger,” she said, referring to the US president’s so-far thwarted attempt last month to bar reporters from several news organisations, including CNN, from accessing the White House.

Can an editorial independence board protect CNN and CBS?

One condition of the settlement requires Skydance to establish a “News Editorial Independence Board” within 180 days of completing the takeover.

The five-member body is to include active or retired journalists with at least 10 years of experience. It is intended to establish editorial principles and address disputes involving the news networks and corporate management.

However, its members will be appointed by, and will report to, Skydance’s board of directors, which Ellison chairs. Two members can belong to the same political party, and there is no requirement to publish its findings.

The condition has left critics with a multitude of questions, including: How can a member of an independent editorial board be a member of a political party? How can there be scrutiny if its findings are not public? How can it be independent if it is appointed by a board of directors, themselves appointed by the CEO of the company?

Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, said, “A Paramount-appointed editorial independence board for CNN and CBS is worthless. The fish rots from the head, and this particular fish is headed by a compromised oligarch with a history of throwing journalists under the bus to advance his business interests.”

Stern also questioned whether government enforcement of the settlement could itself threaten press freedom. “The editorial board creates the same First Amendment problems it’s supposed to solve – the government meddling in the news.”

The First Amendment provides constitutional protection for freedom of speech and the press.

Ellison argues that the two networks will continue to operate independently. “We’re going to make sure that CNN and CBS News are completely editorially independent,” he said on Tuesday.

On Monday, Skydance announced that Mark Thompson would remain CNN’s chairman and editor-in-chief, while Bari Weiss will continue as CBS News’s editor-in-chief, easing previous fears that Weiss would immediately take charge of both networks.

Why are there fears for editorial independence?

The takeover gives the Ellison family control of CNN less than a month before the November 3 US midterm elections, and follows Trump’s repeated attacks on the network as it seeks to hold the US president to account.

Shortly after Paramount launched its bid in December, Trump accused CNN of spreading “poison and lies” and said it was “imperative” that it be sold, while the Trump administration has moved to bar CNN from reporting in certain areas of the White House.

Ellison donated roughly $45m to a political nonprofit group supporting Trump’s election efforts in 2024, while he donated $16.6m to Friends of the Israel Defense Forces, a charity supporting Israeli soldiers – its largest single donation at the time.

Earlier this year, the White House criticised CNN’s coverage of the US-Israeli war on Iran, while Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth told reporters that “the sooner David Ellison takes over that network, the better.”

Sovereign wealth funds from Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates also hold indirect financial interests in the combined company. They have no voting stakes, although their involvement adds another layer of scrutiny over its funding.

Concerns about the future for editorial integrity, however, intensified after Skydance acquired Paramount in 2025, and layoffs followed, alongside the closure of CBS News Radio and changes to CBS News flagship investigative programme 60 Minutes.

High-profile firings enacted under CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss and Skydance Media CEO David Ellison included correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega, as well as 60 Minutes executive producer Tanya Simon.

The programme’s September season premiere attracted about 21 percent fewer viewers than a year earlier.

In 2025, Paramount also agreed to pay Trump $16m to settle a lawsuit over the editing of a 60 Minutes interview with then-presidential candidate Kamala Harris.

In a June 2 letter, nine advocacy groups, including Reporters Without Borders, the Freedom of the Press Foundation and the Committee for the First Amendment, warned that CNN could face similar upheaval and firings.

“Bari Weiss’ shameless actions fulfil the Ellisons’ commitment to President Trump to remake CBS to his liking,” they alleged, referring to the firings and changes at 60 Minutes.

“Larry Ellison has reportedly promised to do the same at CNN if allowed to take control through the pending Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger. Not because it makes any business sense, but because they seek to control the public discourse.”

The groups described the proposed takeover as an “existential threat to the free press, independent media, and free speech in this country and beyond”.

news.title: Democrats have a political violence problem
news.text:
They say politics can be murder. Recent polling suggests a disturbing share of Democratic and left-of-center voters are becoming far too comfortable with the idea.

A new survey from Liberal Currents and the Center for Strategic Politics asked 683 Democratic voters how they would feel about five hypothetical ways President Donald Trump might leave office before his term ends.

Apparently protecting democracy now includes the occasional military junta.

The lawful options drew predictably lopsided reactions: 86% said they would feel positively if Trump were impeached and convicted, and 84% said the same about removal under the 25th Amendment.

Then the poll got darker.

Fifty-nine percent said they would react positively to a headline announcing that military leaders had removed Trump and assumed control of the government to “safeguard the Constitution.” Another 56% said they would react positively if Trump simply died in his sleep.

The only scenario in which negative reactions outnumbered positive ones was assassination. Even there, 31% said they would feel very or somewhat positive if Trump were killed while speaking at a rally; 26% were neutral, and 43% reacted negatively.

The survey measured emotional reaction, not willingness to carry out or personally endorse violence. Still, a positive reaction to an assassination or a military takeover is an ugly result for a party that presents itself as the guardian of democracy.

Apparently protecting democracy now includes the occasional military junta.

Those findings do not stand alone. In April 2025, the Network Contagion Research Institute and Rutgers Social Perception Lab surveyed 1,264 U.S. adults and found that 55.2% of respondents who identified as left of center considered the murder of Trump at least somewhat justified. Nearly 50% said the same about Elon Musk. The researchers described an emerging “assassination culture” among segments of the political left.

Five months later, Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk was assassinated while speaking at Utah Valley University. Prosecutors allege that the accused killer targeted Kirk because of his political and religious beliefs.

RELATED: Where was God? Frank Turek asks the question after Charlie Kirk

 Owen Anderson

The online reaction exposed something broader than one alleged killer’s motive. Social media filled with people celebrating Kirk’s death, mocking his widow, and arguing that he had deserved to die because of his politics.

A YouGov poll conducted after Kirk’s killing found that 16% of liberals said it was usually or always acceptable to be happy about the death of a public figure they opposed. Among the “very liberal,” the number rose to 24%.

Conservatives registered at just 4%.

Cheering a death is not the same thing as committing violence. But political violence becomes easier to rationalize when the target has first been reduced to someone whose death is funny, deserved, or morally cleansing.

I have watched that permission structure develop in my native Portland, Oregon

During the summer of 2020, rioters repeatedly attacked the Mark O. Hatfield U.S. Courthouse with fireworks, incendiary devices, rocks, bottles, and other attempts to set fires. Federal prosecutors charged one man after an incendiary object exploded at the courthouse entrance.

The pattern did not disappear. Beginning in 2025, the Portland ICE facility became another center of unrest. Court records describe protesters throwing rocks and bricks at officers, damaging security equipment, trying to breach the building, and using an upended stop sign as a makeshift battering ram. One participant who struck a federal officer in the head with a rock was later sentenced to 30 months in federal prison.

RELATED: ‘Reign of terror’: One-third of Democrats give thumbs-up to Trump assassination

There is a difference between peaceful protest and political violence. Democrats should be able to draw it without hesitation.

It’s why then-Senator Kamala Harris took flak during the 2020 Black Lives Matter riots when she urged followers to donate to the Minnesota Freedom Fund “to help post bail for those protesting on the ground in Minnesota.” In the middle of widespread disorder, a future Democratic vice president used her platform to promote bail assistance for protesters rather than draw a sharper distinction between lawful protest and criminal violence.

Political violence thrives on permission — explicit or subtle. That permission can come from celebrating an assassination, describing violence as justified, excusing riots because the cause is righteous, or treating the rule of law as optional when the target is sufficiently hated.

Democrats have spent the better part of a decade warning that American democracy is endangered by Trump and the right. They cannot demand that the country take political violence seriously while refusing to confront the appetite for it inside their own coalition.

You cannot save democracy by cheering when your political opponents are removed from it.

That is, in fact, how democracies die.

news.title: Can $1 billion power Republicans to victory in the midterms?
news.text: Republicans are entering the final month of the midterm campaign increasingly anxious that the $1 billion at their disposal may not be enough to fend off sweeping losses as the party reckons with President Trump's unpopularity, persistent cost concerns and the fallout from the war in Iran. The cash advantage, spread out across a half-dozen groups, is driven largely by the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc., which had nearly $416 million in cash on hand at the end of August and began stepping up its spending on critical races in September. But that money may have come too late, forcing the president's group to pay much higher rates because of the shrinking availability of air time. Four Republican Senate campaign officials said groups that reserved advertising time last spring paid much lower rates than MAGA Inc. and its affiliated groups. Instead, by waiting until September, Trump-connected organizations are sometimes paying more than five times what they would have spent if they acted earlier. A representative of MAGA Inc. familiar with the group's strategy said its spending has allowed Republicans to keep races more competitive than they would have been otherwise. In some cases, the group has been the only one on the air criticizing Democratic candidates. The MAGA Inc. representative and the Republican Senate campaign officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal strategy. The challenge is acute in places like Texas, where Trump will travel on Wednesday for the second time in a week to stump for Republican Ken Paxton's Senate campaign. The state hasn't elected a Democratic senator since 1988, yet MAGA Inc. has spent more than $22 million in the past month, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact. Another group, Texas PAC, which is aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, has spent more than $83 million on advertising in the past month, an extraordinary amount to protect what's normally a safe Republican seat. One of those advertisements, which featured Paxton's estranged wife saying she's supporting the full Republican ticket, aired across the United States last weekend during a football game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Houston Texans. Candidates are charged a lower advertising rate than outside groups, so the late infusion of super PAC cash has come at a steep price. MAGA Inc., which is running ads primarily on streaming services, has been charged roughly $894 per airing, according to AdImpact, while Texas PAC has been charged roughly $809 for a mix of broadcast and streaming. That compares with about $290 for Democratic nominee James Talarico's campaign, also on broadcast and streaming. Those averages mask some of the more glaring disparities. For example, during a football game last month, Texas PAC was charged $450,000 to air a single spot in the Austin market. Talarico's campaign paid $50,000 for a spot during the same game in the same market, according to AdImpact. The 2026 campaign is shaping up as a referendum on the power of money in American politics. Democrats freely acknowledge their disadvantage, relying instead on anti-Trump sentiment among voters and targeted messaging on issues like corruption. Some Republicans, meanwhile, are open about the challenge of trying to spend their way out of a tough campaign at this late stage. Neil Newhouse, a longtime Republican pollster, echoed concerns that his party was deploying its cash too late. “After the votes are counted, I think we're going to find the most effective advertising in terms of communicating message and moving voters and poll numbers, the most effective time was advertising that happened well before Labor Day, not after it,” he said. “A million dollars of advertising in October is a drop in the bucket." Thune's group began pulling back in North Carolina last week, a sign of the party's challenge in the Senate race there. The state's outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis has been increasingly vocal about his party's vulnerabilities and recently said that, even with a strong cash advantage, “in the last month, you pretty much have to place your bets.” “If we have endless resources, then we should spend endlessly in every state,” he said. “Absent endless resources, you've got to make data-driven decisions about where you can win.” The midterms mark the first national election since the Supreme Court in June erased limits on how much political parties can spend in coordination with candidates for Congress and president, injecting even more money into a political system already awash in cash. There's plenty of evidence that money alone doesn't translate into victory. Democrat Kamala Harris entered the final stretch of the 2024 campaign with significantly more money than Trump but went on to lose every critical swing state and the White House. Elon Musk's $25 million didn't lift his preferred candidate to a Wisconsin Supreme Court seat last year. And Tom Steyer didn't advance to the general election in the California governor's race despite pumping $216 million of his own money into the campaign. The $1 billion that Republicans have amassed compares with roughly $579 million held by a comparable collection of major Democratic groups. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said his party is facing an “obscene” amount of spending that could swamp them in the midterms. “We're never going to have as much money as them,” he said in an interview. “I sum up the election in this sentence: Can a massive Republican advantage in money beat a massive Democratic advantage in better candidates and political climate? I bet it can't.” In addition to Texas, Democrats have mounted competitive Senate campaigns in states like Ohio, Maine, Iowa and Michigan. A similar dynamic has emerged in governors' races from Florida and Georgia to Wisconsin, Ohio and Nevada. Former President Obama is stepping up his involvement in the midterms and will headline a fundraiser for Senate candidates on Wednesday. In the House, Democrats are growing so confident they can retake the majority that they're expanding their targets deeper into traditionally Republican districts in Arkansas and Tennessee. But a lack of money could limit their gains. “We absolutely need to spend enough to get our message out,” said Rep. Suzan DelBene of Washington, who chairs the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. “And district by district, we are.” From his earliest days as an unlikely political figure, Trump has consistently overcome expectations. Facing daunting prospects heading into the final weeks of his last midterm, he's betting he can again outwit political gravity, relying in large part on the deep bond he's built with supporters. He has stepped up his campaign rallies in recent weeks, traveling to deep red territory to galvanize the party faithful. At events like the one this past weekend in Vandalia, Ohio, the crowd was enthusiastic and cheered at the lines that have become Trump staples over the years, particularly when he dips into profanity. The high school gymnasium that held the event was packed, though crowds began emptying out about halfway through the 90-minute rally. In the closing minutes of a speech Monday in Grand Island, Neb., the president revived his plea that supporters who have stood so fervently by him pretend as if he is on the ballot one more time. “In a true way, I am running,” he said. “We have to keep it going.” Sloan and Beaumont write for the Associated Press. Beaumont reported from Des Moines. AP writers Seung Min Kim in Vandalia, Ohio, and Mary Clare Jalonick in Washington contributed to this report.

news.title: What Was Hope Walz Thinking When She Posted This Photo of Her Dad?
news.text:
Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D-Minn.) ran an impressive race on Sunday, and the internet can't stop staring at his shorts.

Walz ran the Twin Cities 10 Mile for the second straight October with his daughter, Hope, as part of the annual Twin Cities Marathon Weekend. The scandal-plagued governor crossed the line in 1:26:15, an 8:45-per-mile pace, which put him 2,134th out of 9,559 finishers. Hope, 25, came in eleven seconds behind him at 1:26:26, an 8:46 pace, placing 2,164th. 

Now, props to him. Seriously. He's clearly been improving himself and looks more fit than he did on the campaign trail in 2024. A year ago, he ran the same race with Hope in 1:38:12, so he shaved almost twelve minutes off his time. I couldn't run that fast for ten miles. I couldn't run ten miles at all, at this point. I’ve run 5Ks and even trained to do a 10K, but I was never that fast. My best timed 5K came in at roughly a 9:29 pace, and there's no way I could match that now, though I'm working on it. So I'm in no position to heckle a 62-year-old man for not only completing a 10-mile run, but completing it that fast.

ICYMI: James Talarico's Campaign Goes MIA. What's Going On?

But what I’m actually here to talk about is a photo Hope shared on Instagram from after the race. It’s a doozy, and it has social media buzzing. It shows the two of them after the finish, and the governor has a conspicuous, large wet spot on his shorts that makes it look like he wet himself during the run. 

Ummm... @Tim_Walz I have some questions. https://t.co/wTBcmBPBrC— Matt Margolis (@mattmargolis) October 7, 2026

Ten miles is a long way, and the porta potty lines at these things are brutal. Especially if Graham Platner is around, though I'm pretty sure he wasn't at the race.

When I first saw the image, it showed up in my feed as a screenshot. I assumed it was photoshopped or AI-altered. That's the safe bet with anything this convenient. I mean, there’s no way that Walz’s daughter shared that image, right? Wrong. Sure enough, if you go to Hope Walz's Instagram post, you can see the stain as clear as day. So, yes, I can confirm the photo is legitimate. 

View this post on Instagram

What I can't confirm is where the stain came from.

The internet has reached its verdict. Users quickly pointed it out and mocked Walz in the comments.

"I have never ever seen a sweat stain look like that in my 8 years of running in the army," one user wrote.

"Tampon Timmy sprung a leak! We sure dodged a huge bullet on that one!!! Pfhew!!" said another.

"This is the picture you chose?" a third asked.

Other commenters reached back to Walz's 2024 stint as Kamala Harris' running mate.

"I knew he was wearing diapers when he was running with Kamala," one mocked.

"The comments write themselves...this is the pic you chose to post?" another commenter added. "And it never dawned on you that it looks like tampon tim actually needs one?"

Politicians spend fortunes managing their image, and Walz allegedly fancies himself as a potential 2028 presidential candidate (which probably explains why he’s getting in shape). One bad photo can ruin everything — just ask Mike Dukakis or Gary Hart. Clearly, Hope should have reviewed the photo before posting it.

Now, I’m not saying Walz did wet himself. And if the Walzes ever publicly address it, they’ll say it’s sweat, anyway. But still, it’s hard not to laugh.

news.title: Why Paramount-Warner merger has sparked fears about press freedom  - St. Vincent Tribune – Daily St Vincent
news.text:
Paramount Skydance has completed its takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, bringing CNN and CBS News under the same corporate ownership, in a deal that has raised concerns about editorial independence and freedom of speech.

The acquisition, worth about $110bn including debt, combines two of Hollywood’s biggest studios after months of legal challenges lodged by state attorneys general and unions.

The new company, Skydance Corporation, brings together HBO, CBS, Nickelodeon, Showtime, Comedy Central, DC Studios and Food Network, alongside streaming services Paramount plus and HBO Max.

But its control of two major US news organisations has drawn particular scrutiny. David Ellison, Skydance’s chairman and chief executive, has promised to preserve their editorial independence, but his father, Oracle cofounder Larry Ellison is a major financial backer of the deal, and has previously donated funds to US President Donald Trump and Israel.

Asked about the takeover on Tuesday, Trump welcomed it. “They’re terrific people, and it’s going to be a great company,” he said.

Why was the merger challenged?

The takeover faced initial opposition from Hollywood workers, politicians and state prosecutors concerned about the mounting concentration of power in an industry already dominated by a handful of companies.

Netflix initially reached an agreement to buy part of Warner Bros Discovery. Paramount then launched a competing bid, prompting a bidding war before Netflix walked away.

A California-led coalition of 12 state attorneys general sued to block the deal, saying that it would reduce competition and raise prices. The Writers Guild of America brought a separate challenge.

Both cases were settled in September when Paramount agreed to commitments relating to film production, support for displaced workers and protections for the news networks, including the creation of a new editorial independence board.

But the settlement did not end opposition to the deal. “This merger will stifle creativity, weaken free speech and cost people their jobs,” actor and activist Mark Ruffalo has said.

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren linked the takeover to Trump’s efforts to restrict media access. “As Trump tries to ban CNN from the White House, it would be a massive mistake to cave on the Paramount merger,” she said, referring to the US president’s so-far thwarted attempt last month to bar reporters from several news organisations, including CNN, from accessing the White House.

Can an editorial independence board protect CNN and CBS?

One condition of the settlement requires Skydance to establish a “News Editorial Independence Board” within 180 days of completing the takeover.

The five-member body is to include active or retired journalists with at least 10 years of experience. It is intended to establish editorial principles and address disputes involving the news networks and corporate management.

However, its members will be appointed by, and will report to, Skydance’s board of directors, which Ellison chairs. Two members can belong to the same political party, and there is no requirement to publish its findings.

The condition has left critics with a multitude of questions, including: How can a member of an independent editorial board be a member of a political party? How can there be scrutiny if its findings are not public? How can it be independent if it is appointed by a board of directors, themselves appointed by the CEO of the company?

Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, said, “A Paramount-appointed editorial independence board for CNN and CBS is worthless. The fish rots from the head, and this particular fish is headed by a compromised oligarch with a history of throwing journalists under the bus to advance his business interests.”

Stern also questioned whether government enforcement of the settlement could itself threaten press freedom. “The editorial board creates the same First Amendment problems it’s supposed to solve – the government meddling in the news.”

The First Amendment provides constitutional protection for freedom of speech and the press.

Ellison argues that the two networks will continue to operate independently. “We’re going to make sure that CNN and CBS News are completely editorially independent,” he said on Tuesday.

On Monday, Skydance announced that Mark Thompson would remain CNN’s chairman and editor-in-chief, while Bari Weiss will continue as CBS News’s editor-in-chief, easing previous fears that Weiss would immediately take charge of both networks.

Why are there fears for editorial independence?

The takeover gives the Ellison family control of CNN less than a month before the November 3 US midterm elections, and follows Trump’s repeated attacks on the network as it seeks to hold the US president to account.

Shortly after Paramount launched its bid in December, Trump accused CNN of spreading “poison and lies” and said it was “imperative” that it be sold, while the Trump administration has moved to bar CNN from reporting in certain areas of the White House.

Ellison donated roughly $45m to a political nonprofit group supporting Trump’s election efforts in 2024, while he donated $16.6m to Friends of the Israel Defense Forces, a charity supporting Israeli soldiers – its largest single donation at the time.

The programme’s September season premiere attracted about 21 percent fewer viewers than a year earlier.

In 2025, Paramount also agreed to pay Trump $16m to settle a lawsuit over the editing of a 60 Minutes interview with then-presidential candidate Kamala Harris.

“Bari Weiss’ shameless actions fulfil the Ellisons’ commitment to President Trump to remake CBS to his liking,” they alleged, referring to the firings and changes at 60 Minutes.

“Larry Ellison has reportedly promised to do the same at CNN if allowed to take control through the pending Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger. Not because it makes any business sense, but because they seek to control the public discourse.”
