news.title: The Patriot Post® · No, Trump Didn’t Call for Destroying American Cities
news.text:
“Lord, I was born a ramblin’ man,” sang the Allman Brothers Band back in 1973. If anyone can identify with that, it’s Donald Trump.

President Ramblin’ Man struck again on Monday night at a rally in Grand Island, Nebraska. Here’s the relevant portion of Trump’s remarks from Roll Call’s transcript, in which he opined about Iran, high oil prices, nuclear weapons, Los Angeles, and San Diego:

But I want, I wanna see, I wanna see a tremendous victory. You wanna see a tremendous victory, because it verifies all the things we did. And again, remember, with the word, it’s just artificial, it’s a little bit high. It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe.They can take out a city. Let them take, let it, let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That’s, this is a very small price to pay, and it’s gonna be over very soon. It’s essentially almost over with. And they might keep going a little long, you know? They always say they have a big threshold for pain.They need it, let me tell you. They need it. But it’s gonna end very soon, and it’ll end one way or the other, and your gas and your gasoline and all of the things. And don’t forget, we also took on a country known as Venezuela. They never talk about that. They never talk about Venezuela. And we’re taking in hundreds of millions of barrels of oil every week.We’re pouring oil. We’re pouring oil into this country like nobody’s ever seen before.

The New York Times notes, “The audience cheered when he said ‘let them take out Los Angeles; let them take out San Diego,’ and the moment instantly went viral.” The Times isn’t wrong that some in the crowd cheered, though it was nowhere near the whole audience. The story has the video, so judge for yourself. The cheering is, to put it mildly, unfortunate. I’m no fan of LA or San Diego or anywhere else in the Democrat-run People’s Republic of California (go Braves, go Brewers), but cheering for even the vague idea of America’s enemies taking out an American city just shouldn’t happen.

Neither should an American president be so careless with his words, but that’s breaking news from 2017. This is vintage Trump — entertain a crowd with his Ramblin’ Man routine to make his black-and-white divide between how terrible his opponents are and how great he is. Some people love him for it. Others are suffering Trump fatigue.

But for the love of Pete, as the context about oil, Venezuela, and so forth makes obvious, everyone should know that Trump did not mean Iran should take out LA and San Diego.

Yet that’s exactly what Democrats accused him of saying.

“After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California,” California Democrat Governor Gavin Newsom posted on X, “Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego. He is deranged and dangerous.” Elsewhere, he called the president’s comments “treasonous.”

Newsom’s press office then posted, “Let’s be clear: The President is advocating for an attack on 10+ million U.S. residents in two of America’s largest cities.”

Kamala Harris’s “Headquarters” Bluesky account posted, “Trump on Iran: Let ’em take out Los Angeles and San Diego, it’s a small price to pay.”

LA Mayor Karen Bass, who let her city burn while she traveled to Africa last year, was “just shocked” by Trump’s comments and huffed, “It would really be helpful to our city if you would apologize.”

San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria chimed in, too. “San Diego is not collateral damage,” Gloria wrote on X. “We are not expendable. And we are never a ‘small price to pay.’ Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.”

Other Democrats piled on, too, but give me a break. Even the leftists at FactCheck.org get it.

Democrats know full well that Trump’s point, however buried in the word salad, was that high gas prices are a small price to pay to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon with which to take out an American city.

It’s that simple. Why can’t Trump say it that clearly? I have no idea, but Democrats and anyone in the media who amplified it are reprehensible for distorting his comments.

Trump’s military action against Iran is meant to protect America. One terrorist on an Israeli flight nearly did terrible damage. One terrorist with an Iranian nuke could do unthinkably worse.

Republican Congressman Darrell Issa is among those who understand this. “For five decades,” he said, “Americans on American soil have shed blood and lost their lives at the hands of Iran and its terrorist proxies. Where the Obama and Biden Administrations appeased Tehran, paid them billions in bribes, and put them on a glide path to having nuclear weapons, President Trump has taken historic and concrete action to eliminate the nuclear threat, protect every inch of our homeland, and ensure Iran never threatens America or her allies ever again.”

Maybe “Democrats don’t believe the polls,” wonders The Wall Street Journal’s James Freeman. “The leadership of the Democratic Party is so confident of success in November’s elections that they’ve launched an all-hands-on-social-media effort to promote an unbelievable characterization of President Donald Trump’s remarks,” he wrote. “This is not the behavior of people who think they are coasting to victory.”

He may have a point. Yes, Trump rambles and it can be hard to follow, but he clearly was not saying what Democrats accuse him of saying. If they’re so desperate to regain the levers of power in Congress that they’re willing to lie so egregiously about something so simple, what else are they lying about to win an election?

Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, said, “A Paramount-appointed editorial independence board for CNN and CBS is worthless. The fish rots from the head, and this particular fish is headed by a compromised oligarch with a history of throwing journalists under the bus to advance his business interests.”

Stern also questioned whether government enforcement of the settlement could itself threaten press freedom. “The editorial board creates the same First Amendment problems it’s supposed to solve – the government meddling in the news.”

The First Amendment provides constitutional protection for freedom of speech and the press.

Ellison argues that the two networks will continue to operate independently. “We’re going to make sure that CNN and CBS News are completely editorially independent,” he said on Tuesday.

On Monday, Skydance announced that Mark Thompson would remain CNN’s chairman and editor-in-chief, while Bari Weiss will continue as CBS News’s editor-in-chief, easing previous fears that Weiss would immediately take charge of both networks.

The takeover gives the Ellison family control of CNN less than a month before the November 3 US midterm elections, and follows Trump’s repeated attacks on the network as it seeks to hold the US president to account.

Shortly after Paramount launched its bid in December, Trump accused CNN of spreading “poison and lies” and said it was “imperative” that it be sold, while the Trump administration has moved to bar CNN from reporting in certain areas of the White House.

Ellison donated roughly $45m to a political nonprofit group supporting Trump’s election efforts in 2024, while he donated $16.6m to Friends of the Israel Defense Forces, a charity supporting Israeli soldiers – its largest single donation at the time.

Earlier this year, the White House criticised CNN’s coverage of the US-Israeli war on Iran, while Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth told reporters that “the sooner David Ellison takes over that network, the better.”

Sovereign wealth funds from Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates also hold indirect financial interests in the combined company. They have no voting stakes, although their involvement adds another layer of scrutiny over its funding.

Concerns about the future for editorial integrity, however, intensified after Skydance acquired Paramount in 2025, and layoffs followed, alongside the closure of CBS News Radio and changes to CBS News flagship investigative programme 60 Minutes.

High-profile firings enacted under CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss and Skydance Media CEO David Ellison included correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega, as well as 60 Minutes executive producer Tanya Simon.

The programme’s September season premiere attracted about 21 percent fewer viewers than a year earlier.

In 2025, Paramount also agreed to pay Trump $16m to settle a lawsuit over the editing of a 60 Minutes interview with then-presidential candidate Kamala Harris.

In a June 2 letter, nine advocacy groups, including Reporters Without Borders, the Freedom of the Press Foundation and the Committee for the First Amendment, warned that CNN could face similar upheaval and firings.

“Bari Weiss’ shameless actions fulfil the Ellisons’ commitment to President Trump to remake CBS to his liking,” they alleged, referring to the firings and changes at 60 Minutes.

“Larry Ellison has reportedly promised to do the same at CNN if allowed to take control through the pending Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger. Not because it makes any business sense, but because they seek to control the public discourse.”

The groups described the proposed takeover as an “existential threat to the free press, independent media, and free speech in this country and beyond”.

news.title: Can $1 Billion Power Republicans to Victory in the Midterms?
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Republicans are entering the final month of the midterm campaign increasingly anxious that the $1 billion at their disposal may not be enough to fend off sweeping losses as the party reckons with President Donald Trump’s unpopularity, persistent cost concerns and the fallout from the war in Iran.

The cash advantage, spread out across a half-dozen groups, is driven largely by the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc., which had nearly $416 million in cash on hand at the end of August and began stepping up its spending on critical races in September.

But that money may have come too late, forcing the president’s group to pay much higher rates because of the shrinking availability of air time. Four Republican Senate campaign officials said groups that reserved advertising time last spring paid much lower rates than MAGA Inc. and its affiliated groups.

Instead, by waiting until September, Trump-connected organizations are sometimes paying more than five times what they would have spent if they acted earlier.

A representative of MAGA Inc. familiar with the group’s strategy said its spending has allowed Republicans to keep races more competitive than they would have been otherwise. In some cases, the group has been the only one on the air criticizing Democratic candidates.

The MAGA Inc. representative and the Republican Senate campaign officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal strategy.

The challenge is acute in places like Texas, where Trump will travel on Wednesday for the second time in a week to stump for Republican Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign. The state hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1988, yet MAGA Inc. has spent more than $22 million in the past month, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact.

Another group, Texas PAC, which is aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, has spent more than $83 million on advertising in the past month, an extraordinary amount to protect what’s normally a safe Republican seat.

One of those advertisements, which featured Paxton’s estranged wife saying she’s supporting the full Republican ticket, aired across the United States last weekend during a football game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Houston Texans.

Candidates are charged a lower advertising rate than outside groups, so the late infusion of super PAC cash has come at a steep price.

MAGA Inc., which is running ads primarily on streaming services, has been charged roughly $894 per airing, according to AdImpact, while Texas PAC has been charged roughly $809 for a mix of broadcast and streaming. That compares with about $290 for Democratic nominee James Talarico’s campaign, also on broadcast and streaming.

Those averages mask some of the more glaring disparities. For example, during a football game last month, Texas PAC was charged $450,000 to air a single spot in the Austin market. Talarico’s campaign paid $50,000 for a spot during the same game in the same market, according to AdImpact.

Elections are a referendum on the power of money
The 2026 campaign is shaping up as a referendum on the power of money in American politics. Democrats freely acknowledge their disadvantage, relying instead on anti-Trump sentiment among voters and targeted messaging on issues like corruption. Some Republicans, meanwhile, are open about the challenge of trying to spend their way out of a tough campaign at this late stage.

Neil Newhouse, a longtime Republican pollster, echoed concerns that his party was deploying its cash too late.

“After the votes are counted, I think we’re going to find the most effective advertising in terms of communicating message and moving voters and poll numbers, the most effective time was advertising that happened well before Labor Day, not after it,” he said. “A million dollars of advertising in October is a drop in the bucket.”

Thune’s group began pulling back in North Carolina last week, a sign of the party’s challenge in the Senate race there. The state’s outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis has been increasingly vocal about his party’s vulnerabilities and recently said that, even with a strong cash advantage, “in the last month, you pretty much have to place your bets.”

“If we have endless resources, then we should spend endlessly in every state,” he said. “Absent endless resources, you’ve got to make data-driven decisions about where you can win.”

The midterms mark the first national election since the Supreme Court in June erased limits on how much political parties can spend in coordination with candidates for Congress and president, injecting even more money into a political system already awash in cash.

Money alone doesn’t translate into victory
There’s plenty of evidence that money alone doesn’t translate into victory.

Democrat Kamala Harris entered the final stretch of the 2024 campaign with significantly more money than Trump but went on to lose every critical swing state and the White House. Elon Musk’s $25 million didn’t lift his preferred candidate to a Wisconsin Supreme Court seat last year. And Tom Steyer didn’t advance to the general election in the California governor’s race despite pumping $216 million of his own money into the campaign.

The $1 billion that Republicans have amassed compares with roughly $579 million held by a comparable collection of major Democratic groups.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said his party is facing an “obscene” amount of spending that could swamp them in the midterms.

“We’re never going to have as much money as them,” he said in an interview. “I sum up the election in this sentence: Can a massive Republican advantage in money beat a massive Democratic advantage in better candidates and political climate? I bet it can’t.”

In addition to Texas, Democrats have mounted competitive Senate campaigns in states like Ohio, Maine, Iowa and Michigan. A similar dynamic has emerged in governors’ races from Florida and Georgia to Wisconsin, Ohio and Nevada.

Former President Barack Obama is stepping up his involvement in the midterms and will headline a fundraiser for Senate candidates on Wednesday.

In the House, Democrats are growing so confident they can retake the majority that they’re expanding their targets deeper into traditionally Republican districts in Arkansas and Tennessee. But a lack of money could limit their gains.

“We absolutely need to spend enough to get our message out,” said Rep. Suzan DelBene of Washington, who chairs the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. “And district by district, we are.”

Trump turns to his bond with supporters
From his earliest days as an unlikely political figure, Trump has consistently overcome expectations. Facing daunting prospects heading into the final weeks of his last midterm, he’s betting he can again outwit political gravity, relying in large part on the deep bond he’s built with supporters.

The high school gymnasium that held the event was packed, though crowds began emptying out about halfway through the 90-minute rally.

In the closing minutes of a speech Monday in Grand Island, Nebraska, the president revived his plea that supporters who have stood so fervently by him pretend as if he is on the ballot one more time.

“In a true way, I am running,” he said. “We have to keep it going.”

Beaumont reported from Des Moines, Iowa. Associated Press writers Seung Min Kim in Vandalia, Ohio, and Mary Clare Jalonick in Washington contributed to this report.

news.title: Can early votes show who wins midterms?
news.text:
AgenciesWhat is early voting telling us about the 2026 US midterms 

More than 700,000 Americans have already voted in the 2026 US midterm elections across at least 30 states, a month before Election Day on November 3. But early voting figures cannot show which party is winning.The count is as of October 1, according to early vote data compiled by CNN, the Associated Press and the data firm Catalist. Early voting is also underway in Virginia, where in-person voting began on September 18 and runs until October 31, according to local election offices in the state.Democrats gain in ballot requestsCNN's analysis of the data shows Democrats make up a larger share of ballot requests than at this point in 2024 in several states with key Senate or governor races. In Iowa, Democrats account for 67% of requests, up from 54%. In Pennsylvania the figure is 66%, up from 62%, and in Maine it is 57%, up from 53%.Also read: Trump blames France student protests on Islam, migration as US midterms approachLive EventsIn North Carolina, 42% of requests come from Democrats, up from 36% two years ago, according to data from the North Carolina State Board of Elections cited by CNN.CNN also noted that in all these states except Iowa, requests at this point in 2022 were more Democratic than they are now. It said the rise could also reflect Republicans shifting to other ways of voting.Virginia gives the clearest pictureVirginia has reported the most votes of any state in CNN's count. It is the only state with substantial numbers of both early in-person and mail ballots. Virginia voters do not register by party, so CNN looked at how areas voted in 2024. Cities and counties that backed Kamala Harris by more than 20 percentage points are at 78% of their turnout from this time in 2024. Those that backed Donald Trump by 20 points are at 61%.CNN also measured partisan turnout by the share of voters who have taken part only in one party's primaries since 2022. Statewide, Democratic primary participants outpace Republicans by about 18 points, up from 8 points at the same stage in 2024. In two battleground districts held by Republicans, the 1st (Rob Wittman) and the 2nd (Jen Kiggans), Democratic primary participants lead by 15 and 18 points.CNN cautioned that Republican voters could close the gap as Election Day nears. Virginians cast over 4.5 million votes in 2024.Why early numbers can misleadBallots are secret, so the data shows who has voted and not how they voted. The University of Florida's Election Lab, which tracks early voting, says on its tracker that party registration figures are not actual votes. Results will be known only after polls close on November 3.Early voters are also a particular slice of the electorate. CNN exit poll data shows voters aged 65 and above made up 27% of mail voters in 2020, 31% in 2022 and 37% in 2024. CNN said that older share appears to be growing again this year. It added that mail voters have been much more Democratic in recent years, while early in-person voters have been more evenly split or Republican-leaning. Most of the data so far is from mail ballots.A small fraction of the total voteThe votes cast so far are a small share of the roughly 57 million pre-election votes in 2022, according to CNN. The US Election Assistance Commission (EAC) counted more than 112 million ballots overall in 2022, or 46.8% of the citizen voting-age population. The EAC found that 49% of voters cast ballots in person on Election Day that year, and nearly one-third voted by mail.How Americans vote earlyAccording to the Congressional Research Service (CRS), citing the National Conference of State Legislatures, 47 states and Washington DC offered early voting to all eligible voters as of April 2026. Early voting periods ranged from 3 to 46 days. As of June 2026, 37 states and DC offered some form of no-excuse mail voting.Also read: U.S. midterm elections 2026: Are Democrats finally making a comeback in Republican strongholds? Here's what a new midterm poll showsCalifornia, Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Washington and DC hold all-mail elections, and Vermont does so for general elections, the CRS said.Legal changes on mail ballotsOn June 29, 2026, the US Supreme Court ruled in Watson v. Republican National Committee that federal Election Day statutes do not require ballots to be received by Election Day, the CRS said. It added that President Donald Trump's executive orders of March 25, 2025 and March 31, 2026 touch on mail voting. One covers deadlines for returning mail ballots and the other covers the design and transmission of mail balloting materials. Litigation over both was pending as of the CRS's July 10 update.The CNN-compiled count is expected to grow substantially in the coming weeks as more states open in-person early voting.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: 'Disturbing and Dystopian': Trump Latest Agenda Rewards Higher Marriage and Birth Rates With More Funding
news.text: The Trump administration is proposing to give some public transit projects a larger share of federal money based on marriage and birth rates in the areas they serve.Draft guidance from the Federal Transit Administration would raise the federal share for eligible Capital Investment Grants projects by up to 10 percentage points, depending on birth and marriage rates in a project's corridor.The proposal is open for public comment until 16 November and has not taken effect. Democrats have condemned it, with one senior senator calling it 'bizarre and dystopian'.Up to Ten Points for Birth and Marriage RatesThe FTA published the proposed guidance in the Federal Register on 1 October 2026. Under the formula, a corridor with a birth rate more than 1 per cent above the national average would add five percentage points to a project's federal share.A rate equal to or up to 1 per cent above the average would add three points, and a rate within 1 per cent below it would add one point.The same tiers apply separately to marriage rates, so a project could gain up to 10 percentage points combined. Projects below the thresholds would not receive the boost, but the document says they would not otherwise be penalised when their share is calculated.The boost would be added to the score a project receives on existing criteria, and the resulting percentage would determine its federal funding. The calculated amount could not exceed the sum a project requested or the statutory maximum.The proposal cites a Department of Transportation order directing the department, 'to the extent practicable, relevant, appropriate, and consistent with law', to give preference to communities with above-average marriage and birth rates.Billions in Transit Grants at StakeThe Capital Investment Grants programme is a major federal source of funding for large transit projects, including new rail and bus rapid transit lines. Under current FTA policy, the maximum federal grant share is 60 per cent for New Starts projects and 80 per cent for Small Starts and Core Capacity projects.A higher federal share can determine whether a city or region can build a project at all, since local and state governments must find the remainder. On a £2.2 billion ($3 billion) rail line, a 10 percentage point increase would be worth about £221 million ($300 million).The department defended the approach. 'If you want federal funding, your project needs to align with where communities and families are actually growing,' it said in a statement, first reported by Politico on 6 October.The statement added that the department was focused on 'smart, affordable projects with high ridership'.Murray Condemns a 'Bizarre and Dystopian Idea'Senator Patty Murray of Washington, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, called the plan a 'bizarre and dystopian idea you'd expect in a TV show, not actual policy put forth by the US government', The Independent reported.She accused the president of seeking to use the grants for partisan ends. Trump, she said, 'wants to weaponise federal grants to wage his backward culture wars and punish Democrats'.Recent data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have shown fertility rates tending to be higher in Republican-leaning states than in Democratic-leaning ones, and critics have argued that tying transit funding to these measures would favour Republican areas.A Policy First Floated in Duffy's 2025 MemoThe proposal builds on a directive issued by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy shortly after he was confirmed on 28 January 2025.His memo told the department to prioritise communities with marriage and birth rates above the national average, Fortune reported. It also barred recipients from imposing vaccine or mask mandates and required cooperation with immigration enforcement.That directive drew immediate criticism. Murray described it in February 2025 as 'disturbingly dystopian', while Kevin DeGood of the Center for American Progress called it 'bizarre and a little creepy'. Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut said it was 'reminiscent of what you might see in the People's Republic of China' and described it as 'social engineering'.Fortune's analysis of 2022 CDC figures found that all 14 states with the highest fertility rates had backed Trump in the 2024 election, while the 11 states with the lowest rates, along with Washington DC, had supported Kamala Harris. Marriage rates also skewed higher in Republican-leaning states, though by a smaller margin.A White House Focused on BabiesDuffy, a father of nine, urged young Americans in June to 'get married and have lots of kids'. His department's approach mirrors a wider effort within the administration to promote larger families.Trump has described himself as the 'fertilisation president'. In May 2026, the administration proposed a rule concerning employer fertility benefits as part of its push to expand access to in vitro fertilisation.In 2025, the White House also considered proposals such as a $5,000 cash 'baby bonus' for new mothers, CBS News reported, although no such federal payment was adopted.The FTA says the proposed guidance won't take effect until it reviews public comments and finalises the policy, according to its website. Comments are due by 16 November 2026. If adopted, the guidance would make marriage and birth rates in a project's transit corridor a direct factor in calculating its federal grant share.

news.title: Ana Navarro Tells Michael Douglas Why She Remains A Republican On 'The View'
news.text:
Movie legend Michael Douglas halted the gossip for a moment to talk politics Tuesday with co-host Ana Navarro on “The View.”

Just after explaining why he revealed a relationship with “Romancing the Stone” co-star Kathleen Turner in his new book, Douglas pivoted hard.

“I have to ask you something,” he told Navarro. “I’ve admired you now so much for the last couple of years … but why aren’t you independent? How can you still be a Republican?”

Applause and laughter greeted his surprising query.

“I’ll tell you why, because I live in Florida where the primaries are closed, and I want to be able to vote in the primaries and vote against those sons of bitches,” Navarro said. “Make a difference in the primaries.” 

Navarro, a former Republican strategist, has criticized President Donald Trump and his orbit on the show and on CNN, where she sometimes spars with GOP heel Scott Jennings. 

Navarro told Entertainment Weekly last week that she didn’t know if she’d ever change affiliations. She appeared to regret a period as a “Republican hack” who would “regurgitate the same party lines that everybody else regurgitated on TV.”

As for flak from some conservatives that she isn’t a true Republican, Navarro, who supported Democrat Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, snapped back to EW: “I’d argue that anybody who espouses the same views as Donald Trump isn’t much of a traditional Republican. I’m not going to be lectured to about what a Republican is or isn’t.”

news.title: In key Iowa Senate race, Democrat Josh Turek leads Ashley Hinson-Poll
news.text:
In Iowa's crucial Senate race, Democrat Josh Turek narrowly leads Republican Ashley Hinson 48%-44% in a new Suffolk University Poll − one more red flag for Republicans in territory that is typically friendly.

Among the voters Hinson has lost, one in four cite her association with President Donald Trump as the reason.

In the White House race just two years ago, Trump crushed Democrat Kamala Harris in Iowa by 13 percentage points. But unhappiness with his leadership, especially on the economy, has made the Hawkeye state one of the leading prospects for Democrats to flip in their push for control of the U.S. Senate.

The survey of 500 likely midterm voters, taken Oct. 1-4, has a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 points.

Meanwhile, the Iowa governor's race is heading toward a runaway: Democrat Rob Sand has a double-digit edge over Republican Zach Lahn, 55%-43%.

That is notable in a state that hasn't elected a Democrat as governor in two decades.

Trump's red-state itinerary: Nebraska, Texas, Oklahoma

The GOP's heartburn is nationwide.

Trump has embarked on a campaign tour not of swing states but of red ones. He headlined a campaign rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Oct. 5 and was scheduled to hold another Oct. 7 in San Antonio, both states that Republicans traditionally consider safe. A week earlier, he appeared in Oklahoma, Alabama and Ohio.

But Trump's political embrace is a double-edged sword even in such reliably GOP states as Iowa. His favorable-unfavorable rating in the Suffolk poll is a dismal 42%-57%, 15 points underwater. Among Trump's 2024 voters who aren't supporting Hinson now, 24% named as a reason that she was a "sycophant" or "puppet" of Trump.

To be fair, the Democratic candidates in the state don't see the advantage in being joined on the campaign trail by their 2024 nominee. Both Turek and Sand have said they didn't want Harris to campaign on their behalf in Iowa.

Iowa has become one of Senate races that Democrats are targeting in states that had once seemed like long shots, also including Alaska, Ohio and Texas. To win control, Democrats need to flip four red seats and retain all those they hold now.

For Iowa's agricultural economy, Trump's tariffs have hit corn and soybean exports, and the war in Iran has driven up the cost of diesel fuel.

Asked to name the economic issues most affecting their household budgets now, 28% cited grocery costs and another 28% gas and fuel prices. One in five named health care.

In recent weeks, some Iowa GOP officeholders have broken ranks with Trump. Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks in September joined Democrats to support a resolution directing the president to remove U.S. forces from Iran unless he had congressional authorization.

Independents 'turn their backs' on GOP

Turek had the support of 96% of Democrats, Hinson of 87% of Republicans − and GOP voters outnumbered Democrats in the Suffolk survey, 39% to 30%.

But independents gave Turek his lead, splitting 58%-30% in his favor.

"We're seeing independents turning their backs on Republican candidates in three states in a row," said David Paleologos, director of the Suffolk University Political Research Center. "These are the people who swing state elections and they are looking unfavorably toward President Trump, the Iran war, high fuel prices, strained personal finances, and the opposition to federal tax benefits for local AI data centers potentially impacting their water and power grids."

news.title: The Patriot Post® · Trump Shrinks the Federal Workforce
news.text:

Furthermore, what actual “fixes” are the Democrats offering? Higher taxes, even more government handouts, and, of course, the promise of targeting President Donald Trump for impeachment… again. (Apparently, they’re hoping the third time’s the charm.)

So, given the state of this election cycle, it’s worth looking at some of the genuinely significant accomplishments Trump has overseen during his second stint in the White House.

A big one to highlight was the Elon Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE). As is so often the case with politics, there were big promises that didn’t quite materialize — in this case, cutting government spending by $2 trillion.

To put things in perspective, back in 2010 the federal workforce temporarily hit 3.4 million, and in 2020 it numbered 3.2 million. Part of the swell in government employees in those years was due to hiring for the census. However, in January 2025, as Trump was taking office, the federal workforce had swollen to its largest non-census high in 30 years.

Yet by September 2025, the federal workforce had dropped by 150,000 employees. That represents the biggest single decrease in the yearly total of federal employees in almost 80 years. Today, the federal workforce has decreased by an additional 150,000 workers.

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed has a conversation to finish with Michigan Jews | Opinion
news.text:
My father, Eric, died on Oct. 8, 2023, forever linking him in my heart with what happened in Israel the day before. As he lay in his hospital bed on Oct. 7, we watched the news together as the first videos streamed in. He knew he was nearing the end, and I remember him looking up at me and saying, “Well, good luck, Josh.”

Jewish mourning follows a precise calendar. After we buried my father, we sat shiva, the traditional seven days of mourning, with worship services in my home each day. Everyone who gathered with us was grieving both my father and the atrocities of Oct. 7. It was an unexpected gift from my father: a place to share that communal pain.

The last three years have been hard for American Jews. We have felt the pain of Oct. 7, the pain of watching tens of thousands of Palestinians die and the pain of rising antisemitism in our own country. Before Oct. 7, American Jews took for granted our safety, our freedom to define our own identities and our political belonging in a country we’ve called home for centuries. Now many of us who support the State of Israel feel unwelcome in the Democratic Party.

Still Democrats, fighting to belong

And yet, we are still fighting to belong. For decades, roughly 70% of American Jews have called themselves Democrats, and I am one of them. I marched with my family when the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. I raised money for the Black Lives Matter movement. I drove hundreds of miles to help organize a protest at the Tornillo, Texas, detention camp holding migrant children. I did all of this because of the values the Democratic Party best represents.

Register for Opinionated on Oct. 14 to endorsements, the midterms and more with Freep Opinion.

I still agree with 95% of the party’s vision, including the leadership of Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin, and much of Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s thoughtful platform on health care, economic opportunity and democracy. Nearly two-thirds of Jewish voters backed Kamala Harris for president in 2024, according to AP VoteCast. Yet just 15% of Jewish adults say the Democratic Party supports Jewish Americans “extremely” or “very” well, according to an Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll conducted in June. Republicans fare about the same, at 16%. Something is amiss.

The rise in antisemitism makes words matter more

Our community is experiencing record levels of antisemitism. College campuses became an early flashpoint, even before Israel began its military response, as anti-Israel protests gave way to harassment, slurs and threats against Jewish students and university administrators. Hillel International tracked 2,334 antisemitic incidents on U.S. campuses during the 2024-25 academic year, the most since it began tracking in 2019. The latest FBI data found Jews were the victims of nearly 70% of religion-based hate crimes.

More from Freep Opinion: Abdul El-Sayed or Mike Rogers? Freep's pick in U.S. Senate race

Leaders in both major parties have used inflammatory language that risks making things worse. As a lifelong Democrat, I felt obligated to speak up when El-Sayed did the same.

I’m not accusing El-Sayed of being an antisemite. But he has used language that puts my community at risk. Most egregiously, he called Israel “bloodthirsty” on national television after he won the primary. For centuries, accusations of Jewish bloodlust have been used to dehumanize Jews and justify persecution, from medieval blood libels to pogroms to the Holocaust, which killed 6 million of us. There are many legitimate criticisms of Israel’s conduct in this war, but voicing them in language that echoes an ancient antisemitic trope is beyond the pale.

And this was not the first moment that left many Michigan Jews wondering whether El-Sayed understands how his words sound to us. After an armed man drove a truck into Temple Israel in West Bloomfield this spring – a synagogue with a preschool full of children inside – El-Sayed condemned the attack but then spoke about a broader cycle of violence, saying, “hurt people hurt people.” He later apologized for the timing of that comment, saying he had not intended to justify the attack or discount our pain. I appreciated that apology. But his instinct to put what could have been a deadly terrorist attack on the Jewish community into context was worrying.

More from Freep Opinion: Calling Abdul El-Sayed 'antisemitic' avoids the real debate

He describes some American supporters of Israel – a place of importance for many Jews, whether we agree with its government or not – as corrupt and bought by special interests, a dangerous characterization of a complex political landscape.

Of course, I don’t expect every candidate to use precisely the language I would choose. But language from political leaders changes what people regard as acceptable. By using the term bloodthirsty, demonizing American citizens who advocate for Israel and contextualizing the potential murders of preschoolers, El-Sayed has shrunk the gap between criticizing the Israeli government and assigning collective blame to the Jewish community for the Israeli government’s actions. This kind of rhetoric concerns the Jewish community.

Michigan leaders must earn Jewish trust

That matters because senators do more than cast votes on foreign aid. They decide which voices are treated as legitimate, which incidents of hate are condemned, how the government responds when Jewish institutions are threatened and whether Jewish constituents who identify as Zionist are treated with respect within the political ecosystem. I want the people representing Michigan to criticize Israel fiercely, just as I do, when warranted, while also recognizing when rhetoric about Israel – sometimes by their most vocal supporters – jeopardizes the safety of Jews here at home.

I believe the Islamophobic rhetoric of Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers’ campaign is disqualifying. I hold my own party to the same standard. That’s not to say that antisemitic and Islamophobic offenses always take the same form. Often, as we know all too well here in Michigan, Islamophobia is much more overt. But it means political leaders in both parties ought to recognize the histories and hate their words can fuel – and to put their hand up when they get it wrong. El-Sayed owes the Jewish community an explanation for his words during the primary.

Criticizing Israel is not the same as targeting Jews

To be clear, pro-Palestinian views and criticism of Israel are not inherently antisemitic. El-Sayed and I share more common ground than many people realize. As a liberal rabbi in Ann Arbor, I know many of my congregants disagree with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s policies toward Palestinians and the occupied territories. Most of us long for this conflict to end, and we believe Palestinians deserve dignity, safety and self-determination.

More from Freep Opinion: Democracy isn't a trade-off for Jewish safety. It's the foundation

I’ve traveled to Israel seven times since Oct. 7, 2023. On many of those trips, I visited the occupied West Bank and stood in solidarity with Palestinians who are being harassed, beaten and thrown off their land by Jewish terrorists. I donate to organizations working to stop this violence. This winter, I’m leading a congregational trip to Israel and the West Bank to hear from people living with this brutality every day. I refuse to pretend that real suffering doesn’t exist or that this conflict has an easy solution.

I do this work without resorting to rhetoric that echoes antisemitic tropes, and I believe El-Sayed can, too. There is a line between criticizing the Israeli government and casting aspersions on Jews who advocate for Jewish safety in their ancestral homeland. When leaders who seek to represent everyone in this state cross that line, they give radicals permission to hate and alienate a key part of their constituency.

Jewish Democrats don't want to choose between values and safety

At a time when Jews of all ages are being physically and verbally attacked, including at a synagogue 40 minutes from my congregation, rhetoric like this isn’t abstract. It’s terrifying.

It also breaks our hearts, because Jews have been integral to the Democratic Party for generations.

That’s why I helped launch Nonnegotiable Michigan with rabbis and Jewish leaders across the state. We’re asking El-Sayed and other political leaders to commit to principles protecting Jewish safety, identity, political participation and self-determination. We’ve opened that call to Jewish Michiganders and allies through a public petition.

We don’t have to agree on every issue. But we need a starting point to move past harmful rhetoric, open honest dialogue and restore Jewish faith in our leaders. We shouldn’t have to mourn our place in the party we helped build and are still building.

My dad wished me good luck on Oct. 7, 2023, but I don’t think luck is what I need. I need political leaders who go beyond the 95% we already share. I want it all: health care, LGBTQ+ rights, immigrant rights and safety for the Jewish people. I still hope El-Sayed can be that kind of leader. Through understanding and respectful dialogue, we can give this grief what Jewish tradition gives every loss: an end.

Josh Whinston is senior rabbi of Temple Beth Emeth in Ann Arbor. Submit a letter to the editor at freep.com/letters, and we may publish it in print or online.

news.title: Hillary Clinton Endorses Peggy Flanagan In Minnesota Senate Race
news.text:
WASHINGTON — Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton on Wednesday endorsed Minnesota Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan for Senate, making her first congressional endorsement in 2026 and taking a swing at President Donald Trump in the process.

“Donald Trump has made it harder for families to afford childcare, groceries, and health care for their kids. His tariffs and war in Iran are driving up prices, and his budget ripped health care and food assistance away from children so billionaires could get another tax cut,” Clinton said in a statement, first obtained by HuffPost.

“Peggy Flanagan has spent her career fighting for children and families, from the Children’s Defense Fund to the Lieutenant Governor’s office, and she’s delivered for them,” she said. “I know she’ll be that same champion in the Senate, and I’m proud to endorse her.”

Clinton, a former U.S. senator from New York and the 2016 Democratic presidential nominee against Trump, began her career as an advocate at the Children’s Defense Fund. Flanagan, too, is a CDF alum, as the former executive director of the organization’s Minnesota chapter.

“Long before she was First Lady, Senator, or Secretary of State, Hillary Clinton was knocking on doors for the Children’s Defense Fund, making the case that every child in this country deserves a fair shot. That same work shaped me,” Flanagan said in a statement. “Secretary Clinton has spent five decades fighting for those families, and I’m honored to have her support as we take that fight to the United States Senate.”

The Minnesota Democrat has been narrowly leading in the polls against Republican Michele Tafoya, a former sideline reporter for “Monday Night Football” who became a conservative media personality. Flanagan benefits from her state being pretty reliably blue. Voters here went for Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris by more than 4 percentage points over Trump in 2024, and they haven’t elected a Republican to the U.S. Senate in 20 years.

Like Democrats nationally, she also benefits from the president’s approval rating being at an all-time low, with voters saying they are deeply unhappy with the economy, with Trump’s ongoing war with Iran and with corruption in the U.S. government.

Flanagan, a progressive, now boasts the endorsement of both Clinton and her 2016 presidential primary rival, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.).

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report, which closely tracks and rates the political leanings of House and Senate races, rates this seat “likely Democrat” and suggests this race isn’t as close as it might look in polling. It notes Flanagan got a late start to spending in the general election after an ugly Democratic primary against Rep. Angie Craig and that voters here have been uniquely shaped by the hell they endured earlier this year amid the Trump administration’s brutal immigration enforcement tactics that left two Americans dead.

“Given the economy and the state’s ICE raids, this is a difficult climate to try to make a major play in a state Kamala Harris won,” reads Cook’s August analysis of this race.

news.title: Sherrod Brown’s Polling Lead Defies Ohio’s Republican Shift
news.text: Democrat Sherrod Brown’s narrow polling lead in the Ohio U.S. Senate race ahead of the November 3 midterm elections defies the state’s decadelong rightward shift, as Democrats hope to reverse that trend in the Buckeye State this year. Ohio was a premier battleground for much of the 2000s. Former President Barack Obama won the state in both his 2008 and 2012 elections. But it has become increasingly conservative over recent cycles, backing President Donald Trump by 11 points in 2024. Brown, first elected to the Senate in 2006, also went down in 2024, losing his reelection bid to Republican Bernie Moreno. Despite winning by comfortable margins in the past, as the state became more conservative, his personal brand was unable to withstand national headwinds. Two years later, Brown is hoping to score a comeback to make Ohio competitive once again. He is running to unseat Senator Jon Husted, a Republican appointed to fill the seat held by Vice President JD Vance in what has become one of the most hotly contested Senate battlegrounds. Some indications are giving Democrats hope about winning this race. Brown has led in polls and fundraising, and Trump’s declining national approval rating has become a vulnerability for Republicans in close races. Still, a Brown victory would require him to defy the pattern that has seen Ohio become more conservative year after year. Brown’s populist message could be what makes a difference in this year’s elections, Robert Alexander, professor of political science at Bowling Green State University, told Newsweek. Ohio is more of a “populist state than a partisan state,” and Brown “has a known populist brand that has played well with union households, rural voters, and independents.” “Economic populism, resentment toward billionaires and the tech class are messages that resonate with a lot of Ohioans,” Alexander added. “The current backlash against data centers in the state crystallizes all of these concerns and we find that most voters believe that a candidate's stance on data centers is a really important factor in how they will vote.” Newsweek reached out to the Brown and Husted campaigns for comment via email. Sherrod Brown Leads Polls in Close Race Brown has a narrow polling lead about a month out from Election Day. But the race is expected to be among the closest of the midterms, with forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball classifying the battle as a toss-up. The Democratic candidate held a 3.1-point lead in RealClearPolitics’ polling average as of Tuesday. If that holds, the change would mark nearly a 15-point leftward shift from the 2024 presidential race. Brown led by 3 points in the latest survey from The New York Times and Siena University, with 49 percent of respondents saying they planned to vote for him compared to 46 percent supporting Husted. It polled 616 likely voters from September 22 to October 1 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. A Suffolk University poll also gave Brown a 3-point lead, 47 percent to 44 percent. It surveyed 500 likely voters from September 23 to September 27, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. Brown had a more narrow lead in the latest survey from InsiderAdvantage, which showed him up a single point, 44 percent to 43 percent. It polled 1,200 likely voters on September 28 and September 29, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. While Democrats are hopeful about Brown’s lead, polls have underestimated Republicans in the past. In 2024, polls in Ohio showed a modest Democratic bent. Trump was up 7.7 points in 270toWin’s average prior to Election Day, but went on to win by just over 11 points. Brown has also raised significant funds. The Friends of Sherrod Brown campaign committee raised more than $14 million in the second quarter, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings reviewed by Newsweek. His campaign also touted an additional $3 million to other affiliated fundraising committees. Husted’s campaign said he raised $7.7 million across all affiliated committees, including $3.4 million in his principal campaign committee. Ohio’s Race to the Right Trump’s 11-point win in 2024 was the largest Republican margin in decades, underscoring the rightward shift in the state. Obama won it by more than 4 points in 2008 and about 3 points in 2012, before it flipped to Republicans, backing Trump by about 8 points in 2016 and 2020. That trend has been driven by Trump’s inroads with white working-class voters who were previously more politically mixed. His gains came from rural counties as well as the northeastern region near Cleveland. Democrats have gained some ground in Cincinnati and Columbus suburbs, but not enough to offset Republicans' momentum in the rural areas. If Brown wins, he would do so by building a different coalition than the one that backed him in previous races, David Niven, professor at the University of Cincinnati's School of Public and International Affairs, told Newsweek. “The map in Ohio is changing,” Niven said. “Democrats are less dependent on their traditional industrial base and are increasingly counting on a growing suburban base. Places like Delaware County — affluent, educated, white. Delaware has not voted for a Democrat for president since Woodrow Wilson. But that is the kind of place to keep an eye on for Democratic growth.” Alexander said that Democrats will also need to narrow the margins among rural voters. “Rural Ohioans have always voted for Republicans, but their margins of victory have exploded under Trump. This is one of the main areas I will be looking for in this election,” he said. Can Sherrod Brown Reverse Trend? Brown’s candidacy is a major test as to whether Democrats can win back voters in Ohio to stage a comeback in what was once one of the largest, most important swing states in the country. Although he lost in 2024, his performance signals that he still has strength, Alexander said. “Brown outperformed Kamala Harris by a pretty large margin in 2024. While she lost the state by 11 points, he lost by less than 4 points,” he said. “This fact illustrates Brown's crossover appeal as there were somewhere between 200,000 to 300,000 Ohioans who voted for both Donald Trump and Sherrod Brown. This is a remarkable feat in an increasingly polarized era.” Trump not being on the ballot is a major difference, he said. “Trump's popularity is not what it was even two years ago. While he may be able to rally the base, it is worth watching whether his presence stimulates turnout among disillusioned independent voters for Brown.” Data Centers Become Flash Point in Election Artificial intelligence (AI) data centers have become a core issue in Ohio's U.S. Senate race. Husted’s positioning on the centers has become a line of attack for Brown. Husted, as lieutenant governor, was more supportive of data center development in the state. According to the Ohio Capital Journal, he played a role in bringing them there and supported tax breaks for past projects. But he has pushed for some regulations, introducing the Ratepayer Protection Act, which failed to pass the Senate last week. If enacted, it would have required states to consider adopting standards under which large electricity users, including data centers, would pay for the incremental costs of generation, transmission and distribution infrastructure needed to serve them. Democrats opposed the bill, arguing it did not go far enough to address data center concerns. Newsweek's AI Policy Scorecard rates Husted as having a “mixed” viewpoint on AI. Meanwhile Brown has cast himself as a data center skeptic, making standing up to Big Tech a cornerstone of his campaign. “Ohioans are worried about the number of data centers entering our state – I am too. I’m running to take on the big corporations raising our utility bills, defend our resources, and protect our communities,” Brown wrote in a September 19 post on X. Brown’s position on the data centers could be an electoral boon, Niven said. “Brown is benefiting from taking a clear stance opposing data centers, while taking every opportunity to spotlight Husted's long advocacy for data centers. Brown has also tied Husted to political corruption, especially to a bribery case in which Ohioans wound up paying more for electricity because a utility bribed state officials.” Why Ohio Senate Race Matters for 2026 Midterms The Ohio Senate race is among a handful of toss-ups that could determine the balance of power in the Senate. Republicans hold a 53-47 majority that is seen as increasingly at risk in November. Democrats must flip four seats to win a majority, as Vice President JD Vance would serve as the tiebreaker in a 50-50 Senate. Democrats need to flip two seats in states that Trump won by double digits in the 2024 election to secure a majority, and Ohio is viewed as one of those states that could potentially flip to Democrats this year. If Democrats win Ohio, their path to winning a Senate majority becomes more feasible. But if Husted wins, that means they would need to win in some of those other states to regain control of the upper chamber. What Happens Next The Ohio U.S. Senate race will continue to be watched as one of the most competitive of the 2026 midterm elections, as both parties view the seat as crucial come November. news.title: End-of-life doula explains why Congress has a major letting-go problem
news.text:
He’s not the only octogenarian to prevail in a competitive primary in 2026. Eleven won their primaries and are on the ballot for the 2026 midterm elections. The oldest primary winner was Sen. Jim Risch of Idaho, an 83-year-old Republican.

It seems to be an issue both major political parties agree on: For many candidates, age is just a number, even when it starts with an 8 or a 9.

My colleagues and I study succession in family-run businesses and other occupations where leadership, identity and longevity can become deeply intertwined. Whether someone is in charge of a company or is a lawmaker, their work does not only keep them busy. It provides status, an identity and a sense of mission. Letting go means giving up more than a job. 

When business leaders or politicians linger for too long, it can be costly for their companies or constituents because potential successors may become frustrated by waiting and decide to move on.

When any kind of leader remains in their role for decades, underlying reasons can range from a genuine love for what they do to not knowing what they will do – or who they will be – once they leave. However, waiting too long can mean they’ll have to hand off their responsibilities in crisis mode. 

In family businesses, my research team found, the people closest to their leaders – including relatives, employees and longtime supporters – may go quiet rather than press the issue. 

This dynamic is not limited to the business world. It also applies to many of the older members of Congress.

A closer look at the large numbers of legislators who continue to serve during their golden years reflects two trends.

First, many are elected for the first time when they’re middle-aged. New House members were about 50 years old and new senators around 55 in 2025.

Second, although the median age of House lawmakers is now about 60, and 66 in the Senate, there’s a small group of long-serving members who remain in office into and past their 80s and keep running for reelection.

Seeing the advantages of ‘not yet’

Every lawmaker can have a reason to say “not yet.” So can their staff members, who may be loyal to them and their missions and professionally invested in the work they have built together.

Political parties value the electoral advantages of incumbents, while constituents may value the seniority, relationships and influence that come with having spent decades serving in Congress. And incumbents can sincerely believe important work remains unfinished.

However, unusually prolonged service in any position increases the possibility that illness, cognitive decline or death will lead to an unplanned and probably rocky transition.

What’s more, when politicians serve into their late 70s, 80s or beyond, they are breaking with ordinary employment patterns.

The typical American retires in their early 60s, with two-thirds of U.S. workers exiting the labor force before their 65th birthday.

Setting good and bad examples

There are examples of long-serving politicians choosing to plan their exit closer to standard retirement age.

One is Barbara Boxer. After more than three decades in Congress, the 74-year-old California Democrat announced in January 2015 that she would not seek reelection to the U.S. Senate the following year. “There is a time when you want the next generation to step in and step up,” she said.

Boxer’s early decision gave prospective successors nearly two years to organize and voters the opportunity to choose among them. Kamala Harris won the seat but stepped away to serve as President Joe Biden’s vice president.

This departure offers a striking contrast with that of Boxer’s longtime colleague, Sen. Dianne Feinstein, who remained in the Senate through a lengthy health-related absence in 2023. Feinstein, also a California Democrat, died in office that September. She was 90 years old.

She served on the influential Senate Judiciary Committee, which considers federal judicial nominations, including Supreme Court nominees. During her nearly three-month absence, the committee was deadlocked on dozens of Biden nominations after Republicans refused to let the Democrats appoint a temporary replacement for her and she refused to step down.

The tragic way Feinstein’s storied political career ended illustrated what can go wrong when lawmakers keep saying “not yet” until it’s too late.

That turned out to be the case with Biden, who reluctantly ended his presidential reelection campaign in July 2024. However, several books published since then include details about how his inner circle initially advised him to run again. 

A rushed attempt at succession followed Biden’s abrupt withdrawal from the race. Harris became the Democratic nominee without participating in any of the 2024 primaries.

When change finally came, it arrived under duress rather than by design. And Harris lost the election to Donald Trump.

Fearing what might follow

U.S. Rep. Kay Granger, a Texas Republican, announced in 2023 that she would not seek reelection the following year. It soon became clear that severe health problems were preventing her from serving her constituents.

The former House Appropriations Committee chair didn’t cast a vote in her final six months in office for a good reason: She had dementia and was staying in a Texas assisted-living facility that provided memory care services to some residents. Granger died in August 2026 at 83.

U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, a former Senate majority and minority leader, has announced that he will step down when his current term – the Kentucky Republican’s seventh – ends in January 2027. But a fall, hospitalization and subsequent stint in a rehabilitation center in mid-2026 prompted renewed public scrutiny of the 84-year-old’s health and ability to complete his term. 

U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, who turned 93 on Sept. 17, 2026, and appears to be in good health, has not yet said whether he’s running for a ninth six-year term in 2028. But the Republican, who is the oldest person serving in Congress, has urged his constituents to vote for a Republican for governor.

“I don’t plan on dying in office, but if I did, I don’t want a Democratic governor choosing my successor,” Grassley said at a political event in Des Moines in late September 2026.

Learning from palliative care

My colleagues and I found an unlikely way to think differently about leadership transitions: considering lessons about letting go from palliative care.

Leaving political office or another leadership role, of course, is not the same as dying. But, as is true before someone develops a terminal medical condition, advance planning is most useful while people can still articulate what matters to them and exercise meaningful choices about what comes next.

I’ve learned that it’s a mistake to treat succession as something to discuss only when a leader must move on for health or other reasons. So, in addition to my work as a management professor, and to inform my research, as well as the workshops I hold for aging business owners and members of their inner circles, I have been trained as an end-of-life doula. I decided to do this because I lacked the vocabulary and tools that facilitated difficult conversations and decisions about their legacy and what is important to the leader as they let go.

Palliative care supports the act of letting go long before death – the same challenge confronting business leaders and the companies they run. 

When voters consider whether to vote for an aging incumbent, they may wonder whether that lawmaker is already too old for their demanding job or soon will be. But that may be the wrong question. It might be better to ask whether the legislators who represent you, no matter their age, have a plan for letting go.

Nancy Forster-Holt, Clinical Associate Professor of Innovation and Entrepreneurship, University of Rhode Island

U.S. Sen. Ed Markey is 80 and has served in Congress for half a century. His Democratic primary challenger in Massachusetts, U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton, is 47 and made generational change a centerpiece of his campaign. Markey won the Sept. 1, 2026, primary anyway by nearly 30 percentage points.

He’s not the only octogenarian to prevail in a competitive primary in 2026. Eleven won their primaries and are on the ballot for the 2026 midterm elections. The oldest primary winner was Sen. Jim Risch of Idaho, an 83-year-old Republican.

It seems to be an issue both major political parties agree on: For many candidates, age is just a number, even when it starts with an 8 or a 9.

news.title: Trump’s comment about Iran nuking Los Angeles and San Diego was incoherent, not malicious
news.text:
President Donald Trump says many bizarre and even hateful things. But signaling he would allow Iran to nuke Los Angeles and San Diego is not one of them.

During a rally in Nebraska on Monday night, Trump “weaved” his way right into a controversy that had critics, some in the media and even a GOP congressional candidate accusing him of rhetorically conceding major population centers on the West Coast to America’s sworn enemy. And you could be forgiven for reading the president’s comments that way.

But context and recent history make clear that Trump’s crime was less indifference to the fate of Californians and more his increasingly profound incoherence.

Which, to be clear, is still a major problem for the most powerful man in the world.

First, let’s recap what Trump said.

“They can take out a city,” he said of Iran. “Let them take – let it – let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That’s – this is a very small price to pay.”

It wouldn’t be totally out of character for this to be another Trumpian verbal excess, given his recent past. This is a president who has repeatedly spoken about withholding disaster aid from states that vote against his party, and he has demonstrated some indifference to blue states. His Energy Department recently admitted in court that it canceled clean energy grants “based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state.”

Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont accused Trump of saying the small price to pay was the “annihilation of two major American cities.” Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut called it “such a sick, evil thing to say.” Even GOP congressional candidate Jim Desmond, who serves on the San Diego County board of supervisors, said what Trump did was “write off American cities as an acceptable price of war.” Desmond “vehemently” disagreed with it.

But that is pretty clearly not what Trump was trying to say.

For one, immediately before the above quote, he had been talking about other costs of the Iran war — apparently referring to gas prices — being that “small price to pay.”

“And again, remember — with the word — it’s just artificial, it’s a little bit high,” Trump said. “It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe.”

(You can see Trump’s full speech here.)

Trump didn’t initially say he was referring to gas prices, mind you (though he did say that later). But this is precisely how he’s been talking about them for a long time — as a “small price to pay” for preventing a nuclear Iran:

Also, three days ago, Trump made a very similar argument to the one he made about Los Angeles and San Diego — except about Mobile, Alabama, during a rally there.

“But remember about the oil: You’re paying a price, but boy, is that a small price than what it would be if these lunatics were allowed to have a nuclear weapon and used it on Mobile, Alabama,” Trump said. “OK, not going to happen.”

At his Nebraska rally, Trump basically took that talking point and made it a whole lot more unintelligible.

He bounced around from talking about Kamala Harris and the election, to wanting total victory in Iran, to talking about gas prices being high (but without actually saying “gas prices”). When he made the comment about Iran nuking Los Angeles and San Diego, he used very unfortunate sentence construction that did sound a lot like he would “let them” — Tehran, that is — nuke the two blue state cities.

And then he returned to the gas prices — but again, in an extremely confusing way.

“But it’s gonna end very soon, and it’ll end one way or the other, and your gas and your gasoline and all of the things —” Trump said, before jumping off on a tangent about Venezuela.

It was so confusing that not only did that GOP congressional candidate seem to interpret it in the worst way; so did many in the crowd. Indeed, the ugliest part of this whole episode is that people actually cheered when Trump floated the destruction of Los Angeles and San Diego. That would seem to say something about the movement Trump has cultivated.

But while he wasn’t advocating that, his phrasing does point to a growing problem.

A president is someone you count on to be authoritative and clear, especially when talking about issues of the utmost importance like nuclear war. But Trump’s rhetoric is often anything but.

Look at any recent interview where a transcript is released. Some of Trump’s responses in his Time magazine interview last week, for example, are virtually impenetrable. (Just do a word search for “unintelligible” if you want some examples.) It often feels like he’s engaging in a lengthy bout of free association.

Trump has long spoken like this, to an extent. And by casting his meandering soliloquies as “the weave,” he’s tried to make it sound intentional, allowing his supporters to believe it’s his secret rhetorical genius.

But the “weave” is getting harder to follow — with potentially harmful consequences, too.
