news.title: Blue wave is rising in Senate races
news.text:
While states like North Carolina and Georgia seem firmly in the Democratic column, states in which Republicans seemed like a lock even just a few months ago are becoming competitive. As the Times article about pulling ad funding from North Carolina noted, the GOP Super PAC will be diverting some of that money to Kansas. Democrats have not won a U.S. Senate election since 1932. That's right, 1932.

The quality of a candidate matters and in Kansas the Democrats nominated Adam Hamilton, pastor of the largest church in the state. He is facing incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall who appears to spend more time in Florida than in Kansas. Hamilton made headlines last week when he declined to have either former Vice President Kamala Harris or Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer come to Kansas and campaign for him. Trump beat Harris there by a whopping 57% to 41% in 2024.

Texas is another state in which Republicans have been sailing to victory in recent decades. In 2024, Trump won all but two of the counties along the Rio Grande, counties with large Hispanic populations which had traditionally voted for Democrats. In 2016, Hillary Clinton carried all but three of the border counties. The population of the Diocese of Brownsville, which contains the two most eastern counties along the border, is about 85% Catholic. If they swing back to the Democratic column, Democratic nominee James Talarico could be on his way to the Senate.

As in Kansas, candidate quality matters in Texas. The Republican nominee, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, was impeached by the GOP-controlled House of Representatives in Austin in 2023, accused of abusing the power of his office. The Texas Senate ultimately acquitted him. Talarico has made mistakes, but even his most egregious ones ("God is nonbinary," he said in a floor debate in the Texas legislature) were well-intentioned.

Talarico is a seminarian in the Presbyterian Church. It is noteworthy that two of the Democratic Senate candidates who have created a real shot for themselves are so overtly religious. Talarico is more liberal than Hamilton, and Republicans have been attacking him as a heretic, but the New York Times' David French posed the right question: "Will Talarico's religious faith help put him — and his party — over the top?" Liberal or not, Talarico's frequent invocation of Scripture distinguishes him from the caricature of a liberal, East Coast elite. And, unlike Kansas, it will be Catholics along the Rio Grande who may decide the election.

Democrats should not count their proverbial chickens before they hatch. As CNN's Harry Enten recently pointed out, polls have failed to predict Republican turnout in recent elections. In 2024, Republicans outperformed the polls by 9 points in Iowa, by 6 points in Ohio and by 5 points in Michigan.

Trump was on the top of the ticket in 2024, but the polls were also off in 2018, the midterm held during Trump's first term. Then, Republican candidates outperformed the polls by 6 points in Iowa, by 6 points in Ohio and by 8 points in Michigan.

Religion would not even be a factor in these Senate races if the economy were booming or if the Iran War had gone as promised. But the economy is not booming and the Iran War is a mess. Catholics will play almost no role in Kansas, but will in North Carolina and Michigan. In Texas, they could be decisive. The election is still a month away, and any candidate is always just one banana peel away from disaster. But the Democratic wave is rising, and some of the winds causing that rise are religious, and specifically Catholic breezes.
news.summary: "The blue wave is rising, and while it may not lift all boats, it is apparently lifting some. And religion is part of the story," Michael Sean Winters writes.
news.author: Michael Sean Winters

news.title: Philadelphia teacher passing as Palestinian raised alarms for Jewish groups before she rose to fame
news.text: The first time most of the world heard Hannah Gann's name was in late September, when the 34-year-old Philadelphia high school teacher and activist confessed to having fabricated a Palestinian and Black identity — with media reports revealing she was Jewish in real life. But Jason Holtzman, director of Philadelphia's Jewish Community Relations Council, first heard Gann's name long before that: in December 2023.At that time, he recalled to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, she “made some pretty strident remarks” at a local rally called “Flood Philly For Palestine,” an apparent reference to the “Al-Aqsa Flood,” Hamas's name for its Oct. 7, 2023, attacks.In a video from the event shared with JTA, Gann said in reference to children in Gaza, “We owe them to take it to the streets and f–k the police until Palestine is free.”Gann would appear on the JCRC's radar several more times before her name hit the news for being “the Palestinian Rachel Dolezal,” when her story — accompanied by Philadelphia Inquirer reporting that she has Jewish family living in Israel — ricocheted across the internet to gain her instant notoriety. (The real-life Dolezal, a white woman who posed as Black for years and held a NAACP leadership role while teaching Africana Education at a Pacific Northwest college, has meanwhile expressed interest in meeting Gann.)Gann's revelations have led to the dissolution of the local pro-Palestinian educators group she had helped to lead since 2024. After leaving her Instagram confessions public for more than a week, Gann's account was deactivated in the last few days.Yet now that Gann's background has grabbed headlines, Jewish groups alarmed by her behavior said the real story is being missed. “It's just being reported as if she simply is guilty of fraud, that she's the new Rachel Dolezal,” Holtzman told JTA. “It's missing part of the story, which is that she's also an extremist who has spread antisemitic tropes and has brought inflammatory content into the classroom.”A general view of the School District of Philadelphia offices on December 31, 2015 in Philadelphia City. (Paul Marotta/Getty Images)A catalog of troubling incidentsIn the JCRC's monitoring of the School District of Philadelphia, Gann's name pops up often. In 2024 she helped organize a pro-Palestinian “teach-in” project, an unofficial event staged for teachers in the district that the JCRC says “directed educators to materials that erased Israel from maps” and “characterized October 7 as 'resistance.'” That year she also posted an Instagram image of a fist rising from the ground holding a firearm, with paragliders — a symbol of the Hamas attacks on Oct. 7, 2023 — visible in the background, one of many social media posts of hers that employed extreme language or imagery around Israel. A key part of Jewish critics' charges, that Gann brought her activism into the classroom or into her lesson plans, is harder to pinpoint. But in one screenshot of her whiteboard that she posted to social media, Gann appeared to have planned a lesson on “Black Power & Palestine.” In addition, district personnel who had visited her class in 2024 found that it “contained a 'Palestine will be free' poster, a Palestinian flag, a keffiyeh, and a map of Israel filled with a keffiyeh design,” Holtzman claimed. Gann did not respond to multiple JTA requests for comment. JCRC officials and a local Jewish activist group had pushed the district to discipline Gann over her conduct before the scandal over her identity broke — including, they said, presenting the superintendent with a full record of Jewish parent concerns this March. But such efforts, they say, fell largely on deaf ears. “We've pointed this out to the school district many times over the years,” Holtzman told JTA. He added that, in the JCRC's view, Gann's rally appearances and social media activity were in violation of district codes of conduct governing staff activity that could damage the district's reputation — with her recent admission of falsifying her ethnic identity potentially violating an ethics code requiring employees to avoid falsification in their personal records.“And they've basically done nothing about it,” he said.It wasn't only Holtzman and the JCRC urging the School District of Philadelphia to take some kind of action against Gann. Local Jewish activists filed a federal civil rights complaint against her and fellow activists in the district with whom she had formed a coalition, even entering into mediation with the district in an effort to establish new guidelines around personnel behavior. The complaint argued, among other points, that Gann's social media — where she has posted many controversial messages about Israel — should be considered an extension of her classroom.Yet Gann continued to teach 10th grade at The Workshop School, a public high school in West Philadelphia with a focus on project-based learning. Under pressure from her fellow activists, she recently came clean about her identity. A surprising confession“I lied about my family and have been lying for years,” she wrote on Instagram on Yom Kippur. “I have no Palestinian or Tunisian heritage. I am a white woman of significant privilege and wealth. Anyone who supported me was manipulated.”Gann's confession took even the Philadelphia Jewish groups who had been tracking her behavior by surprise. They told JTA they had not realized she had been identifying herself as Palestinian, nor that she was actually Jewish. Some of her fellow activists, in their own social media posts, said she had confided to them in the past that she was Jewish — while also continuing to insist she was Palestinian. While the Philadelphia Inquirer has quoted activists accusing her of having “Israeli settler family,” it was unclear to the Jews who spoke to JTA whether Gann's Israeli family actually lived in settlements in the occupied West Bank or whether the activists simply refer to all Israelis as settlers. Giving public comment at prior school board meetings, Gann had proclaimed, “I can't visit my family in Palestine,” and “I have pushed myself to teach through the agony of my family living in a warzone, and only taken one day off this entire school year.”To some Jews, such parsing is almost beside the point; they see the entire conversation around Gann's identity as a distraction. The bigger story, they said, is that she was using her position as a public school educator to push anti-Israel advocacy that included falsehoods about Israel without fear of punishment: a microcosm of what they see as a larger trend of growing pro-Palestinian sentiment among K-12 educators in many school districts and teachers' unions that has raised alarm among Jewish groups.A spokesperson for an ad hoc group of Jewish educators and families in the Philadelphia area, who asked to remain anonymous owing to what they viewed as death threats from a member of Gann's former coalition, told JTA in a statement that the district failed to express interest in Gann until the scandal.“Harm to the Jewish community is never addressed or rectified” by the district, the representative for the School District of Philadelphia Jewish Family Association (SDP JFA) said in an email.A spokesperson for the School District of Philadelphia declined to comment on whether the district would be disciplining Gann or if it had communicated with Jewish groups about her behavior prior to last week.“The District is making support available to the Workshop School staff and students, as needed,” the spokesperson wrote in an email to JTA.Meanwhile, one of the pro-Palestinian activist groups formerly associated with Gann, Philly Educators for Palestine, announced last week that “after much reflection,” it would dissolve, though “The work continues.” Its parent group, the Racial Justice Organizing Committee, said it would be going on hiatus.Prior to its announcement, Philly Educators for Palestine had publicly disassociated from Gann and had called for the district to discipline her. “It's one of the first times where I think that I really have common ground with the Philadelphia Educators for Palestine,” Holtzman quipped. Pro-Palestinian demonstrators block roads as they rally in front of Philadelphia City Hall in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on September 10, 2024, ahead of the presidential debate between US Vice President and Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris and Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump. (Andrew Thomas / AFP via Getty Images)Civil rights complaint filedIn 2024, SDP JFA filed a Title VI civil rights investigation with the U.S. Department of Education against a group of pro-Palestinian teachers in the district, alleging, among other things, that students had been targeted on the basis of their Jewish identity. Joining the complaint were the JCRC, the Anti-Defamation League and StandWithUs, a pro-Israel advocacy group. The groups eventually proceeded to mediation with the district, which agreed to institute changes such as drafting a district-wide anti-harassment statement; undergoing an anti-discrimination policy review; and instituting new training for staff, according to a copy of the resolution agreement viewed by JTA. Jewish groups, however, charge that the recommendations were never fully implemented.The names of the teachers in the federal investigation were redacted in official filings. But according to emails shared with JTA, Gann was one of the named parties in the ADL's amended complaint. “Evidence suggests that Ms. Gann is utilizing her actual classroom and social media platforms as a digital extension of her classroom to disseminate antisemitic rhetoric, engage in prohibited political campaigning, and promote extremist ideologies to her students,” a letter sent by SDP JFA this May reads. Following that email, Gann on Instagram made oblique references to the allegations, calling her unnamed critics “genocide enthusiasts who love to call the School District about what I'm teaching.” She also posted a fake lesson plan from her classroom whiteboard with scheduled “lessons” including “Jesus Was Palestinian.”The Jewish parents and teachers in SDP JFA say their frustrations with Gann are also informed by an even more antagonistic encounter with Keziah Ridgeway, a fellow teacher and former ally of Gann's who at one point had joined Gann in holding signs reading “From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free” at a school board meeting. In 2024, following a controversy around one of Ridgeway's lesson plans and an SDP JFA campaign against her, Ridgeway, believing herself targeted by Jewish online harassers, posted several of the group members' names to Instagram. In posts viewed by JTA, she accompanied this list with another post referencing the phrase, “Ain't no fun when the rabbit got the gun,” which refers to a sudden reversal in power dynamics. In a third post, Ridgeway asked followers for recommendations for “Black owned [gun emoji] shops in or near Philly.” The Jewish parents interpreted the series of posts as a threat directed at them, and reported Ridgeway to the district, ultimately leading to her suspension for a year; she has sued the district, alleging anti-Islamic bias. Gann forcefully advocated for Ridgeway's reinstatement at board meetings. Following Gann's recent revelations, Ridgeway, too, disowned her in an Instagram video. “I can no longer be in community with someone who caused so much harm,” Ridgeway wrote on social media.Ridgeway declined to comment to JTA, citing ongoing litigation.Even if they feel it's for the wrong reasons, the members of SDP JFA still want to see action taken against Gann. They are seeking to capitalize on her newfound infamy by renewing their calls to district officials to discipline her and “ameliorate the damage done to the Jewish community.” Such demands echo communications Jewish parents have sent to the district for the better part of two years. In an email to administrators last year, they sought to sum up their complaints: “Allowing Ms. Gann to remain in a teaching position sends the message that Jewish students' safety and dignity are not valued — that their teacher can publicly call for their eradication without consequence.”
news.author: Andrew Lapin/jta

news.title: GOP Sen. Susan Collins nudges Trump to stay away from Maine: ‘I’m not exactly his favorite senator’
news.text:
WASHINGTON — Sen. Susan Collins seemingly had a not-so-subtle message for President Trump: stay away.

During her first debate of the cycle against Democrat Troy Jackson, Collins (R-Maine) twice dodged a question on whether she would stump with Trump if her were to swing through the Pine Tree State.

“I don’t think that President Trump is going to come to Maine,” she replied when asked. “He’s talking about going to a lot of different states. I’ve heard nothing from his office. And I’m not exactly his favorite senator.”

Pressed again, she replied, “I would say that he is not coming to Maine.”

On Monday, Trump indicated to reporters that he was planning to swing through Maine as part of his midterm blitz, but so far, no concrete plans for such a trip have emerged publicly. 

“I think we’re going to Maine too. I’m going to Michigan in a week and a half,” Trump said.

Trump lost Maine to former Vice President Kamala Harris by about seven points in 2024. Maine has gone blue in all presidential elections this century. However, the state’s Republican senator has managed to hang onto her seat during that time.

Trump had loomed large over Collins’ debate against Jackson, who tried to blame her for some of the president’s policies, such as the war in Iran, the trade war with Canada, and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Collins repeatedly distanced herself from Trump, underscoring how she opposed him on all three of those issues. She highlighted a study that found she “voted against my party more than any other senator on either side of the aisle.”

She also touted her efforts to mitigate problems she claimed came from Maine’s Democrat controlled state government and Trump. At one point, she noted how she negotiated to get salt removed from the tariff list, noting Maine’s dependence on imports from Canada to treat its roads in the winter.

“What about everything else? We can’t eat road salt,” Jackson fired back. 

As Jackson tried to blame the people of Maine’s problems on chaos in Washington, Collins worked to redirect fire on him and state governance in Augusta.

“If you look at the policies that have driven up the cost of living in Maine, you have to look at Augusta. Maine has the fourth-highest electricity rates in the country. It has some of the highest housing costs in the entire country,” she said. 

“It has extraordinarily high property taxes. Those are all due to Augusta’s failed policies under the failed leadership of Troy Jackson.”

Jackson, who relied heavily on a thick white binder full of notes during the verbal bout, led the state Senate from 2018 through 2024. But Collins highlighted his struggles to pass significant legislation.

Perhaps his biggest gripe against Collins was her vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court in 2018. Jackson pressed her about what “will it take for you to admit you are ever wrong?”

“I clearly don’t agree with how Brett Kavanaugh voted on Roe v. Wade,” she said at one point. “I would point out that there’s only one of us on the stage who has always been pro-choice, and that’s me.”

Early in his political career, Jackson took staunchly pro-life positions, but later changed course and became pro-choice.

She also pointed out that she voted for all of the liberal justices on the Supreme Court.
news.summary: During her first debate against Democrat Troy Jackson, Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) twice dodged a question on whether she would stump with Trump if her were to swing through the Pine Tree State.

news.title: Can $1 billion power Republicans to victory in the midterms?
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Republicans are entering the final month of the midterm campaign increasingly anxious that the $1 billion at their disposal may not be enough to fend off sweeping losses as the party reckons with President Donald Trump's unpopularity, persistent cost concerns and the fallout from the war in Iran.

The cash advantage, spread out across a half-dozen groups, is driven largely by the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc., which had nearly $416 million in cash on hand at the end of August and began stepping up its spending on critical races in September.

But that money may have come too late, forcing the president's group to pay much higher rates because of the shrinking availability of air time. Four Republican Senate campaign officials said groups that reserved advertising time last spring paid much lower rates than MAGA Inc. and its affiliated groups. 

Instead, by waiting until September, Trump-connected organizations are sometimes paying more than five times what they would have spent if they acted earlier. 

A representative of MAGA Inc. familiar with the group's strategy said its spending has allowed Republicans to keep races more competitive than they would have been otherwise. In some cases, the group has been the only one on the air criticizing Democratic candidates. 

The MAGA Inc. representative and the Republican Senate campaign officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal strategy.

The challenge is acute in places like Texas, where Trump will travel on Wednesday for the second time in a week to stump for Republican Ken Paxton's Senate campaign. The state hasn't elected a Democratic senator since 1988, yet MAGA Inc. has spent more than $22 million in the past month, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact. 

Another group, Texas PAC, which is aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, has spent more than $83 million on advertising in the past month, an extraordinary amount to protect what's normally a safe Republican seat.

One of those advertisements, which featured Paxton's estranged wife saying she's supporting the full Republican ticket, aired across the United States last weekend during a football game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Houston Texans. 

Candidates are charged a lower advertising rate than outside groups, so the late infusion of super PAC cash has come at a steep price. 

MAGA Inc., which is running ads primarily on streaming services, has been charged roughly $894 per airing, according to AdImpact, while Texas PAC has been charged roughly $809 for a mix of broadcast and streaming. That compares with about $290 for Democratic nominee James Talarico's campaign, also on broadcast and streaming. 

Those averages mask some of the more glaring disparities. For example, during a football game last month, Texas PAC was charged $450,000 to air a single spot in the Austin market. Talarico's campaign paid $50,000 for a spot during the same game in the same market, according to AdImpact.

Elections are a referendum on the power of money

The 2026 campaign is shaping up as a referendum on the power of money in American politics. Democrats freely acknowledge their disadvantage, relying instead on anti-Trump sentiment among voters and targeted messaging on issues like corruption. Some Republicans, meanwhile, are open about the challenge of trying to spend their way out of a tough campaign at this late stage.

Neil Newhouse, a longtime Republican pollster, echoed concerns that his party was deploying its cash too late. 

“After the votes are counted, I think we're going to find the most effective advertising in terms of communicating message and moving voters and poll numbers, the most effective time was advertising that happened well before Labor Day, not after it,” he said. “A million dollars of advertising in October is a drop in the bucket."

Thune's group began pulling back in North Carolina last week, a sign of the party's challenge in the Senate race there. The state's outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis has been increasingly vocal about his party's vulnerabilities and recently said that, even with a strong cash advantage, “in the last month, you pretty much have to place your bets.”

“If we have endless resources, then we should spend endlessly in every state,” he said. “Absent endless resources, you've got to make data-driven decisions about where you can win.” 

The midterms mark the first national election since the Supreme Court in June erased limits on how much political parties can spend in coordination with candidates for Congress and president, injecting even more money into a political system already awash in cash. 

Money alone doesn't translate into victory

There's plenty of evidence that money alone doesn't translate into victory.

Democrat Kamala Harris entered the final stretch of the 2024 campaign with significantly more money than Trump but went on to lose every critical swing state and the White House. Elon Musk's $25 million didn't lift his preferred candidate to a Wisconsin Supreme Court seat last year. And Tom Steyer didn't advance to the general election in the California governor's race despite pumping $216 million of his own money into the campaign.

The $1 billion that Republicans have amassed compares with roughly $579 million held by a comparable collection of major Democratic groups.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said his party is facing an “obscene” amount of spending that could swamp them in the midterms.

“We're never going to have as much money as them,” he said in an interview. “I sum up the election in this sentence: Can a massive Republican advantage in money beat a massive Democratic advantage in better candidates and political climate? I bet it can't.”

In addition to Texas, Democrats have mounted competitive Senate campaigns in states like Ohio, Maine, Iowa and Michigan. A similar dynamic has emerged in governors' races from Florida and Georgia to Wisconsin, Ohio and Nevada. 

Former President Barack Obama is stepping up his involvement in the midterms and will headline a fundraiser for Senate candidates on Wednesday. 

In the House, Democrats are growing so confident they can retake the majority that they're expanding their targets deeper into traditionally Republican districts in Arkansas and Tennessee. But a lack of money could limit their gains. 

“We absolutely need to spend enough to get our message out,” said Rep. Suzan DelBene of Washington, who chairs the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. “And district by district, we are.”

Trump turns to his bond with supporters 

From his earliest days as an unlikely political figure, Trump has consistently overcome expectations. Facing daunting prospects heading into the final weeks of his last midterm, he's betting he can again outwit political gravity, relying in large part on the deep bond he's built with supporters.

He has stepped up his campaign rallies in recent weeks, traveling to deep red territory to galvanize the party faithful. At events like the one this past weekend in Vandalia, Ohio, the crowd was enthusiastic and cheered at the lines that have become Trump staples over the years, particularly when he dips into profanity. The high school gymnasium that held the event was packed, though crowds began emptying out about halfway through the 90-minute rally. 

In the closing minutes of a speech Monday in Grand Island, Nebraska, the president revived his plea that supporters who have stood so fervently by him pretend as if he is on the ballot one more time.

“In a true way, I am running,” he said. “We have to keep it going.”

This story has been corrected to show Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said, “I bet it can’t,” not “I bet it can.”

Beaumont reported from Des Moines, Iowa. Associated Press writers Seung Min Kim in Vandalia, Ohio, and Mary Clare Jalonick in Washington contributed to this report.
